label.en: The Australian government should fund a childcare program for every child in Australia.

analystStatement.en: “The Coalition supports an early childhood education system which is responsible, measured and provides support to families who need it most,” [Shadow Minister for Education] Senator Henderson said.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition believes taxpayer support for childcare should be means-tested and retain an activity test to target the highest support to lower income families and those who work the most hours. Our previous reforms locked in ongoing funding for preschools and kindergartens, and increased access for more than 280,000 children.

analystStatement.en: Anthony Albanese [Party Leader and Prime Minister]: “Every child should have the right to quality, affordable early education. That’s why we want to build a universal child care system that is simple, affordable and accessible, for every family. We think children should have guaranteed access to at least three days of high-quality early education and care – because early education is about changing lives.”

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government believes every child should have the right to quality,  affordable early education. That's why we are working to build a universal childcare system that is simple, affordable and accessible for every family and where every child is guaranteed access to at least three days of high-quality early childhood education and care. We have announced a new $1 billion Building Early Education Fund to build new centres in areas of need and increase the number of childcare places available.

analystStatement.en: Changes that would allow most parents to access three days of subsidised child care a week, regardless of whether they are working or not, could pass through federal parliament within weeks [...] [Green] Party leader Adam Bandt said the party was willing to work with the government if it wanted to pass the bill quickly. "If the government wants to get legislation through this fortnight to go some way towards what the Greens have been calling for — and make child care and early childhood education accessible and affordable to everyone in this country — then we're prepared to work with them and make it happen," he said.

partyStatement.en: All children, no matter their primary carers’ income, employment status or postcode, deserve the best start in life. We need a free and universal early years education system, just like we have with schools.

analystStatement.en: “One Nation wants to give wage earning couples with families a choice to file tax returns separately or together,” [One Nation leader Pauline Hanson] said. “In many cases it would save couples a considerable amount of money in terms of their taxes, providing immediate and much-needed cost-of-living relief. It can also encourage couples to start families sooner because they can better afford it, and reduce childcare costs for the government by better enabling one partner to stay at home if they choose.”
According to Judith Sloan, the cost of Universal Childcare works out to be more than $200,000 per job created. Doesn’t seem like the best use of taxpayer dollars to me.

partyStatement.en: I would support a small user-pays component

analystStatement.en: The government stalled its own early childhood education bill – but I pushed them again to act, and it has now passed! Early Childhood Education and Care gives kids the best start, supports families, and boosts productivity. The next stop is low, flat fee universal access.

partyStatement.en: Yes, over time. This will benefit children, families and the economy. It involves large structural change to a complex system and supply side issues have to be resolved so it's not an overnight change.
The Australian government already funds childcare for the vast majority of Australian children. I would like to see it become more accessible and more affordable.
Universal early learning and care holds significant benefits to our children's development which in turn benefits, our community, our economy and our society.

Bob understands society has become so expensive that it is nearly impossible for families to live on single incomes. Both parents have to work - for many families, this isn't a choice. For this reason he supports reliable access to quality child care for working parents but would prioritise supporting flexible, children at work arrangements and income splitting and financial support for stay at home mothers and carers.
Funding a childcare program for every child in Australia isn't financially sustainable. Families should be prioritised according to needs.

label.en: How much should the Australian government spend to subsidise the cost of electricity for consumers?

analystStatement.en: Opposition Leader Peter Dutton says the [Labor government's] budget had been described by economic commentators as a "disaster", despite flagging support for some of the announcements. "We'll support those measures. Because I think a lot of Australians are hurting a lot more than what we might realise at the moment," Mr Dutton told AM. The energy bill relief, $300 for households and $325 for around 1 million small businesses, will go straight onto bills. It's an expansion of a 2023-24 budget measure that was limited to 5 million eligible households.

partyStatement.en: Australian households and businesses are paying amongst the highest energy prices in the world. Labor promised to reduce annual electricity bills by $275, but electricity prices have skyrocketed under Labor. Instead of fixing the underlying problem, Labor has spent taxpayer funding to mask them with temporary, and inflationary, subsidies. The Coalition will deliver affordable and reliable energy with a balanced energy mix of renewables, gas, storage and zero-emissions nuclear.

analystStatement.en: The government will extend rebates on electricity bills by six months, providing another $150 cut to power bills for households and small businesses. The rebates will be automatically applied to every household and about 1 million small businesses from July 1, and applied over two quarterly instalments. Treasury estimates that cost-of-living relief will directly reduce headline inflation by about half a percentage point in 2025, and household bills by 7.5 per cent on average — at a cost to the budget of $1.8 billion over the forward estimates.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government has taken comprehensive steps to address cost-of-living pressure - including three rounds of energy bill relief that have provided hundreds of dollars of support to every single Australian household and to small businesses. We know families are feeling the pinch - that is why we are delivering cheaper, cleaner, more reliable energy that brings down costs for households and businesses, capitalises on Australia's renewable resources, and puts cost-saving energy efficient technologies directly into the hands of more Australian consumers.

analystStatement.en: Mehreen Faruqi [Greens Deputy Leader]: "The Greens recognise that cost-of-living relief is so desperately needed, and that's why we are supporting this [Energy Price Relief Plan] bill. [...]  So of course this scheme, this plan, this legislation is not enough, and there is much, much more to do. [...] The government should really listen to the Greens and freeze power bills for two years. We will keep pushing for this freeze so people can have much more meaningful cost-of-living relief."

partyStatement.en: By shifting to renewable energy and “electrifying everything” we can not only drive carbon pollution to zero, but we can lower home energy bills and industry costs while creating jobs around the country. In this term of Parliament, the Greens have secured $800 million for life-changing energy upgrades to public and social homes, saving people $1,800 a year on their energy bills.

analystStatement.en: One Nation considers there would be little to no need to subsidise electricity costs by abandoning net-zero policies, abolishing subsidies for large-scale renewables, withdrawing from the Paris Agreements and prioritising more reliable and cheaper gas and coal power generation.

partyStatement.en: One Nation considers there would be little to no need to subsidise electricity costs by abandoning net-zero policies, abolishing subsidies for large-scale renewables, withdrawing from the Paris Agreements and prioritising more reliable and cheaper gas and coal power generation.

analystStatement.en: Whether you sit in the fossil fuel or renewables camp is irrelevant here. In plain terms – at the moment, everyone’s losing. We’re seeing higher energy bills. We’re seeing Aussie taxpayers funding unviable subsidies and policies, and we’re seeing approval ratings for renewable and fossil fuel companies alike dropping fast. We need to cut through all this mess and focus on what really matters to everyday Australians: access to cheap, reliable power.

The $300 energy rebate may technically reduce the measure of inflation, but it seems like a blunt instrument, not being means tested. [...] My Priorities[:] [...] Reduce energy bills through household electrification & energy efficiency support.

partyStatement.en: Government has a role to play in supporting the transition to the cheapest source of energy, renewables, rather than subsidising electricity on an ongoing basis. This will lower costs over time.

Government funding should be going into supporting households and small businesses to electrify via solar and battery storage, switch to heat pumps and efficient appliances and new builds need to be built to higher efficiency standards. This will reduce the need to be giving energy bill relief by creating permanently lower bills.
I'm calling for the government to subsidise batteries for households and businesses to lower the cost of electricity for all consumers by discharging cheap electricity back to the grid.

The government should pursue policies that permanently reduce power bills, through support for rooftop solar, home batteries and more efficient appliances. My Permanent Energy Bill Relief Plan sets out a blueprint for this and would help over 800,000 households.

analystStatement.en: The Government assisted cost-of-living with [...] energy relief to all households [...] and [...] small businesses. [...] The energy relief for households is [...] welcome. [...] $300 energy bill relief for every household, $325 energy bill relief for some small businesses [but] [...] Nil for electrification of household and long term energy cost relief.

partyStatement.en: The Government should prioritise spending on modernising our grid and transitioning to renewables to lower the cost of electricity for consumers.
Any concessions should of course be targeted at those most in need of energy bill relief.
Australia needs to stop its blinkered approach to achieving net zero and reinvest in affordable energy solutions such as reliable coal fired power generation.

label.en: Political parties should commit to running at least as many women candidates as they do men.

analystStatement.en: Opposition Leader Peter Dutton says he wants more Liberal women in federal parliament, but local branches were selecting candidates who have a strong affinity with their communities. [...] Women comprise about 30 per cent of its MPs and senators in the federal parliament compared with 52 per cent of Labor seats held by women. Asked about the figures on Tuesday, Mr Dutton said he wanted to see more Liberal women running in seats but also pointed to his new candidate for Blair, Carl Mutzelburg, as an example of someone who was able to garner the support of his local community. “Communities respond to local members who have an affinity with their community, who have delivered, who have a real passion about fighting for the priorities of that local community,” he told reporters while campaigning in the outer Brisbane electorate. [...] “In our party, we have a democratically based process where our members make decisions about who the candidates will be. In the Labor Party, the faceless union bosses decide who will be the candidates. Ours is a much more democratic process. Of course, we want to see more women running in seats, and we have got some incredible candidates.”

partyStatement.en: The Coalition is committed to strong female representation at all levels. We are proud to have appointed Australia's first women Ministers for Foreign Affairs, Defence and Financial Services. The Liberal and National Parties believe the best candidates are selected by local members through democratic pre-selections. The Liberal Party's Federal Executive has adopted a target of 50% female representation within our Parliamentary ranks within ten years or three terms, and to adopt practical measures to increase the female representation in the Parliament as quickly as possible.

analystStatement.en: In 2002 the ALP introduced a 40 per cent quota for party positions, union delegations and for pre-selection for public office and positions at a State and federal level, building on a 35 per cent quota introduced in 1994. Either of the sexes shall be represented by no less than 40 per cent on party electoral lists. (National Platform and Constitution 2009, Article 10a.) The ALP has adopted a 50 per cent gender diversity target for government boards to be achieved within the first term of a Labor government and 40 per cent for women's representation in Chair and Deputy Chair positions on government boards by 2025 (National Platform 2018)

partyStatement.en: The Australian Labor Party has a long-running commitment to affirmative action  and a 50% target for women's representation which we have reached ahead of schedule. 53% of Commonwealth Labor MPs are women and in the 47th Parliament the Australian Labor Party formed the first Commonwealth Government with a majority women members.

analystStatement.en: The Australian Greens want: [...] Affirmative action initiatives which facilitate the equal representation and participation of women in public life, employment, and cultural and social opportunities, including women from diverse backgrounds.

partyStatement.en: The Australian Greens prides itself on being a progressive organisation both internally and externally. Currently more than half of the Australian Greens MPs are women, and all the candidates running in target seats are women.

analystStatement.en: We advocate for policies that [...] promote fairness and common sense over divisive identity politics.

partyStatement.en: Parties should be making internal decisions about how to address any gender imbalance in their candidates, but if they choose not to, voters can look outside the party system to support gender equity.
It's really up to the parties. If they don't commit to it, it's a reflection on them. It then becomes a factor for those who vote for them, or not!
Of course this is decision for each party, but I believe any party that doesn't have broadly equal representation will need to explain why to voters.

analystStatement.en: Aside from conducting inquiries, electing more women to parliament, there is a need for a cultural change, [Independent MP Zali] Steggall said. “But you also then have to look behind the curtain of the proportion of women at senior roles at their unions and their whole party structure,” Ms Steggall said. “It’s also not just about having more women in the chambers as MPs or senators. It’s also more female heads of departments, it’s more female chiefs of staff, chief advisers, experts. It’s universities – we need more women as professors – you know, it’s across the board. “If you have much more equitable gender representation and cultural representation, because I also think parliament is incredibly lacking in cultural diversity – until you achieve a better reflection of society, I don’t think you have a system best placed to come up with best laws for society.”

partyStatement.en: Ensuring there is diversity - gender, age, race and ability - across parliament is important to maintaining strong representation of our society.
It should always be based on merit. The best person for the job.
More should be done to encourage women to seek election. However, this should not be at the cost of merit.

label.en: Transgender women should be able to compete in women’s sporting leagues.

analystStatement.en: [Opposition Leader] Peter Dutton has shut down his Nationals counterpart's suggestion that Australia should "lean into" the gender debate, after Donald Trump's executive order rejecting recognition of transgender people in the United States. [...] "Australia is a sovereign nation, and as prime minister I'll act in our country's best interests, and I'll make decisions that I think are in the best interests of all Australians," Mr Dutton said. "We don't have any plans to change our position in relation to that issue."

partyStatement.en: The Coalition believes women and girls should be able to compete in a fair and safe environment. Women having to compete against individuals with an unfair biological advantage goes against the spirit of sport.

analystStatement.en: [Prime Minister Anthony] Albanese [...] [said] that it's up to the organisations to contend with the issue and that Australia’s sporting codes are able to “deal with it” if needed.

partyStatement.en: The Government does not set policy for gender eligibility in sport but the Australian Sports Commission does have guidelines that help sports develop their own policies. It is a matter for each sport to determine policies  regarding gender as relevant to their sport, and within Australian laws.

analystStatement.en: The Australian Greens want: [...] The removal of discrimination against transgender and gender diverse athletes, and athletes with variations in sex characteristics in competitive and community sport.

partyStatement.en: Trans women are women. We will always fight changes to legislation that seek to make it harder for trans, gender diverse and non binary people to participate in sport.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "In the past, women were excluded from sport so they took their bat and ball and formed their own competitions and teams. The recent success of women’s competitions in footy demonstrates how far we’ve come in Australia. However, sport is meaningless unless it’s fair. Allowing trans women to compete in women’s sport is not. It undermines and contradicts the entire concept of sport. If trans women want to play sport, they should do what women did before them – take their bat and ball and form their own competitions and teams. Give them an inch in women’s sport and they will take a mile, but not if I have anything to say about it."

During the 20th century women fought hard to secure fundamental rights and freedoms including the vote. But it seems there is a new battle being fought – a fight to protect women-only spaces. These spaces play a vital role in ensuring the privacy, security, and safety of women. The recent Tickle v. Giggle case has brought this issue into sharp focus. This case involved a legal challenge to the exclusion of males from the women-only social media platform Giggle. The women lost. At the heart of this case is Australia’s Sex Discrimination Act 1984, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex, gender identity, and sexual orientation. But the Act also recognises the need for single-sex spaces. For example, Section 33 protects women-only spaces or services, such as shelters, changing rooms, bathrooms, toilets, and women’s sport. These provisions exist to protect privacy, safety, and equality for women. The law recognizes that these exemptions are important for safeguarding hard fought for women's rights. And yet the court’s decision failed to uphold this.

partyStatement.en: There needs to be an individualised approach to transgender participation based on fairness.
This is a matter for the sporting codes under guidelines developed by the Australian Sports Commission.
It is most appropriate for individual sporting leagues to determine this for their own sporting league and not for the government to decide.
The conduct of sporting competitions should be left to the sporting codes. They should not be politicised.
I believe individual sporting codes should continue to regulate their own elite level competitions as required.
The governing bodies of individual sports and medical professionals are best placed to determine the rules around this.

analystStatement.en: [Independent MP Zali] Steggall said there was "no issue" in women's sport, which was well regulated by national sporting bodies. "They have policies to ensure inclusive opportunity in sport when it comes to a community level, and fair participation in sport when it comes to an elite level," the former Olympian said.

partyStatement.en: All Australians should have the ability to engage in sport. It is my view that the current protections in legislation and in the codes of the various sporting bodies provide adequate guidance and protection for athletes of all genders and allow for discretion at the community sport level which is important for the mental and physical health of all citizens. Sport Australia has an established diversity policy and Sport NSW have also established a useful set of guidelines available.

label.en: The Australian government should help university graduates pay off their student loans.

analystStatement.en: [Opposition Leader Peter Dutton]: "When [Queensland Premier] Steven Miles was deeply unpopular, he went on a spending spree to try and help him reset and gain his popularity back. [...] Mr Miles was willing to sacrifice the state's finances to try to make people like him again. The Prime Minister played this card trick on the weekend with his $16 billion university degree debt policy. Prime Minister, our country is off track, and this Labor government is damaging the economy and keeping interest rates higher for longer, which is hurting families. When will the reckless spending stop?"

partyStatement.en: Australian taxpayers currently pay 60 per cent of a university student’s education, recognising the important benefit that higher education provides to both individual students, and to our country. We support students repaying their income-contingent student loans at a level that is sustainable for graduates, based on their income thresholds, and for taxpayers. But Labor's plans to spend $16 billion cutting debt for some students is unfair to the 24 million Australians who don't have a student loan, including those who have already paid off their loans. As leading economist Chris Richardson says: ‘…handing $16bn to graduates is a reverse Robin Hood: it’s a tax cut targeted to the big end of town, with money going from the less well off to the better off’.

analystStatement.en: Three million Australians will see $3 billion wiped from their student debt after the Albanese Government passed legislation through the Parliament tonight. This legislation fixes the way indexation is calculated on student debt and will be backdated to 1 June 2023.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government is committed to making the education system fairer and more affordable. We have already wiped $3 billion from the student debts of 3 million Australians and have committed to cut a further 20% off all student debts in a second term to alleviate pressure on students.

analystStatement.en: [T]he Greens have announced an election plan to wipe all student debt, unshackling almost 3 million people from their debts and allowing people to keep more of their paycheck. [...] The Greens have relentlessly pushed the Albanese Government to deliver desperately needed student debt relief since they came to power [...] All student debt should be wiped.

partyStatement.en: At a time when skyrocketing student debt is making the cost-of-living crisis worse, the Greens have announced an election plan to wipe all student debt, unshackling almost 3 million people from their debts and allowing people to keep more of their paycheck. The Greens have relentlessly pushed the Albanese Government to deliver desperately needed student debt relief since they came to power, and the pressure has worked. We are proud of this win but let’s be clear — Labor’s plans still fall short of what’s needed. All student debt should be wiped and university and TAFE should be free. This is a start, but if Labor can wipe 20% of student debt, surely they can wipe all of it.

analystStatement.en: One Nation does not believe we should forgive HECS or HELP debt. People have a duty to pay off their loans. However, there are some issues with how indexation is applied to the HECS-HELP debt. [...] If you have to pay for it out of your own pocket, you will work harder to achieve your goals. Nothing's free, at all, in this country. Taxpayers work hard. They put their taxes towards providing these universities for these students. That's why students should be able to pay their way. A system where they don't start paying it back until they start working is fair. It won't be abused, then, if they have to pay their way.

So, [in the 2024-25 Budget] I was pleased to see the government take on board key policies that I’ve advocated for over the past two years – namely calls to [...] reduce HECS [student loan] debts for our young people.
As your Curtin Independent MP, I’m proud to have helped deliver results for our community. $3bn in student debt relief for 3 million Australians.

partyStatement.en: Investing in education is good long-term thinking. We need cheaper higher education and a clear plan for funding it.

analystStatement.en: I support the restoration of funding for tertiary education and research to levels commensurate with our standing as a prosperous and innovative nation. Research and development is especially critical to our future when it comes to climate and renewable energy.

partyStatement.en: Restructuring the way that HECS debts are calculated via the timing of HECS indexation would alleviate pressure on students, as well as making sure banks don't factor HECS debt into granting of mortgages.

We need a fairer university fee system that prevents students incurring large debts in the course of their studies rather than bandaid solutions that require government intervention after the debt has been incurred.

analystStatement.en: At the moment, HELP loans are adjusted annually on June 1, meaning the debt continues to increase without taking into account what people have already paid off in tax during the financial year. The debts, also known by their old name of HECS, are tied to inflation rather than wages growth. [...] Crossbenchers including Dai Le and teal independents Zoe Daniel and Allegra Spender have urged the Government to fix this by immediately adopting recommendations from the Universities Accord.

partyStatement.en: Younger Australians are struggling at the moment and HECS is one part of the problem, particularly the Job Ready graduate scheme is burdening particularly arts students. I am open to reforming university funding models to help younger Australians.

analystStatement.en: It is positive to see the Government finally heeding the calls of many to fix the broken HECS system. But we still need the Government to go further. Debts are indexed on 1 June of each year. Repayments taken by the ATO throughout the year are not applied to reduce the balance of the student debt until lodgement of income tax returns, after 1 July every year. The repayments are not applied to reduce the debt prior to the debt being indexed. This needs to change. Either repayments withheld by the ATO are applied in real time to decrease the debt balance prior to indexation or the indexation date should be moved to a date after the end of the financial year.

partyStatement.en: The Australian government must fix the inequitable indexation of student loans, which would indirectly assist students to pay off their loans. I strongly support the policy to remove HECS-HELP from debt-to-income reporting and serviceability assessments. The Australian Government should reverse the changes made by the Morrison Government to the cost of non-STEM degrees and should make university degrees more affordable.
Subsidies should be guaranteed for Australian citizens. All Australians have a right to education regardless of their bank account.

label.en: How much funding should non-government schools receive from the Australian government?

analystStatement.en: “Not only do non-government schools support parental choice, but they also play a vital role in taking funding pressure off the government school sector. The government has a responsibility to protect the funding mechanisms which are critical to the viability of low fee-paying schools particularly in regional and remote Australia where student numbers are reduced and capital is scarce,” [Shadow Minister for Education Sarah] Henderson said.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition supports parents choosing the best school that suits their family and will deliver Commonwealth funding for all schools fairly and sustainably, based on students needs, and also taking account of the income level of the parent community contributing to the school. The Coalition has no plans to change the current policy.

analystStatement.en: At the moment, non-government schools are funded at the Schooling Resource Standard, or they are on track to get there, or they are above it and coming back down to it. Most public schools aren’t. The Commonwealth Government provides 80 per cent of the SRS funding for non-government schools and the State and Territory Governments provide the other 20 per cent. For public schools it’s the reverse. The Commonwealth provides 20 per cent of the SRS funding, and the States and Territories are supposed to provide at least another 75 per cent. That means there is a five per cent gap. The Albanese Government has put $16 billion of additional investment for public schools on the table to help fill that gap.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government believes parents have a right to choose a non-government school. Non-government schools should be supported by public funding that reflects need.

analystStatement.en: Decades of underfunding have left public schools struggling to meet the needs of their students while elite private schools enjoy taxpayer-funded luxuries. Unlike Labor and the Liberals, who have failed to address the growing inequity in education, the Greens are committed to fully funding public schools and ending wasteful subsidies for the wealthiest private institutions.

partyStatement.en: The Greens will continue funding non-government schools and want to see every school, particularly underfunded public schools, funded to the level that they need, which means to 100% of their school resource standard. The Greens also want to stop government overfunding and that will mean some very wealthy private schools receive less taxpayer funding. The Greens want to see a well funded public education sector, with a significant boost in funding for public schools.

analystStatement.en: One Nation supports public funding of both government and non-government schools; competition ultimately leads to better standards for all students.

partyStatement.en: Between State and Federal governments, support should be available for the education of every child in Australia.

analystStatement.en: I believe that people have a choice regarding where they send their children to school, be it private or public. [...] School funding should be equitably distributed across the education sector; however, disadvantaged schools and special needs programs should be prioritised. All children deserve an equal opportunity in education regardless of where they live, what their parents earn, or whether they are educated in public or private schools.

partyStatement.en: As States do not provide funding to non-government schools, federal funding is necessary to ensure that non-government schools have adequate resources for all Australian students to receive high-quality education. Although, it is important to ensure equitable outcomes between non-government and government schools. A full implementation of the Gonski Review, which focuses on ensuring that all Australian students have the opportunity to achieve their very best regardless of their background or circumstance, should be prioritised.

label.en: Australia should build nuclear power plants to generate electricity.

analystStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition Government will: [...] Establish a civil nuclear program in Australia, including operating nuclear power plants in seven locations across the country.

partyStatement.en: Nuclear energy is at the heart of our plan to provide affordable and reliable energy for Australian families, and our heavy industry and manufacturing sector. Unlike Labor's "renewables-only" approach, the Coalition will deliver a balanced energy mix with renewables, gas, storage and zero-emissions nuclear.  Nuclear provides the “always-on” power needed to back up renewables, stabilise the grid, and keep energy affordable. Advanced economies worldwide are expanding nuclear programs to meet their energy and emissions goals, and Australia must not be left behind.

analystStatement.en: Anthony Albanese [Party Leader and Prime Minister]: "Here's the lowdown on nuclear power. It will add $1,200 to your power bills. It will take decades to build. It will block cheaper renewable energy. Energy experts at the CSIRO and the Australian Energy Market Operator have made that clear. Still Peter Dutton is asking Australians to pay the price for his nuclear power scheme. Never before has so much taxpayer money delivered so little to so few Australians. Australia needs cheap, clean power now, not expensive power decades down the track."

partyStatement.en: Nuclear energy is wrong for Australia - it takes too long, costs too much, and will  drive energy prices up for Australian households and businesses. Relying on nuclear would mean curtailing household solar, pausing the roll-out of low-cost renewables, and extending the life of expensive, aging and unreliable coal plants. It would cost taxpayers at least $600b, increase energy bills by $1200, and cut off the economic and industrial opportunities of a renewables-powered economy - as well as leading to higher carbon emissions indefinitely.

analystStatement.en: The only way to keep people safe is a massive expansion of renewable energy. [...] No nuclear. And no more coal and gas.

partyStatement.en: Dutton’s dangerous nuclear agenda will delay action. The only way to keep people safe is a massive expansion of renewable energy.

analystStatement.en: One Nation supports nuclear energy in principle but we do not consider there is a pressing need for it considering Australia has plenty of coal and gas to generate cheaper and more reliable energy.

partyStatement.en: One Nation supports nuclear energy in principle but we do not consider there is a pressing need for it considering Australia has plenty of coal and gas to generate cheaper and more reliable energy.

analystStatement.en: Nuclear energy in Australia will be too slow to deliver with a 15+ year timeframe from the time of a decision to proceed and is too expensive as it is the most expensive form of new energy.

partyStatement.en: While nuclear may make sense at some point, currently the economics don't stack up.
Not ideologically opposed to nuclear energy, it simply doesn't stack up for Australia now on timing, cost or against other readily available renewable options.
However, small modular nuclear reactors may have a role to play in the future for hard to abate sectors.

I am technology agnostic but the numbers on nuclear don't add up. It is too expensive and slow and would lead to more coal and gas in the next 10 years, which will be expensive for Australian families. We should stay the course and provide certainty to investors.

analystStatement.en: [Independent MP Zali Steggall]: "You can’t claim to care about the cost of living while promoting nuclear power for Australia. Peter Dutton’s nuclear plan would hit Australians hard—doubling power bills for solar households and undermining energy efficiency savings, leaving families paying more for less. Experts agree renewables are the cheapest, most reliable solution, already driving bills down across the nation. The good news is that renewables already power 40% of our energy, nearly half way there. Now is the time to accelerate the transition with smart solutions, not go off track!"

partyStatement.en: The CSIRO has found that nuclear power plants would cost twice as much as renewables and would take longer than the 15 years proposed by the Liberal Government, reducing our opportunity to achieve net zero by 2050. Australia’s only pathway for cheaper, clean energy is with renewables. The Climate Change Authority has found that building to nuclear would lead to an additional 2 billion tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions from the energy sector by 2050 as it would delay roll out of renewable energy and possibly limit quantity of renewable energy into the grid.

analystStatement.en: Invest in nuclear power. Nuclear is clean, reliable, low carbon and easy to ramp up and ramp down subject to demand.

partyStatement.en: In appropriate locations, nuclear is a reliable, affordable and suitable solution. Coal fired power should be the priority.

I am open to having a national conversation about nuclear power as part of a broader discussion about energy, particularly given that nuclear power complements renewable energy in many similar developed nations. We need to examine whether nuclear power would be financially viable for baseload power/manufacturing, however this should not delay us from renewable energy projects supported in the community.

label.en: The government should ban the expansion of coal mining operations in Australia.

analystStatement.en: The Coalition argues coal-fired power stations do not need to be, and should not be, phased out as soon as is now planned by AEMO.

partyStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition Government stands unashamedly with Australia’s resources sector. A strong resources sector not only provides jobs in local communities around Australia, but also underpins Australia's economic strength to support investments in the services that Australians rely on every day, including roads, hospitals, and aged care. In terms of coal fired energy generation, we need new baseload reliable energy generation to replace retiring coal-fired power plants, and we have a plan to address these challenges through a balanced energy mix with renewables, gas, storage and zero emissions nuclear.

analystStatement.en: The Albanese government has approved the expansion of four coalmines that climate campaigners estimate will release more than 850m tonnes of CO2 over their lifetime – equivalent to almost double Australia’s annual emissions. The four mines will target mostly coal to be used for steelmaking with some thermal coal for burning in power stations. [...] [Environment Minister Tanya] Plibersek attempted to downplay the decisions, saying the projects were “all extensions of existing operations” and were producing coal for making steel that was essential for “homes, bridges, trains, windfarms, and solar panels”. “There are currently no feasible renewable alternatives for making steel,” she said. She said the projects would support up to 3,000 jobs and had to comply with Australia’s commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2050. The government had issued “240 strict conditions across the projects to ensure the environment is protected,” she said. The projects would be assessed under the government’s revised safeguard mechanism, which only accounts for emissions generated in Australia. The bulk of the emissions caused by the projects come when the coal is burned overseas, and is therefore not counted under Australia’s climate commitments.

partyStatement.en: Through our Future Made in Australia plan, we are investing billions in production  incentives for green hydrogen, critical minerals, solar and battery supply chains. Decisions to expand a small number of coal mining operations, primarily for metallurgical coal for use in steelmaking which currently has no low-carbon alternative, are made on a case-by-case basis in accordance with state and Federal law, and emissions are regulated under the Safeguard Mechanism.

analystStatement.en: [Adam Bandt]: "Australia is on fire, fuelled by coal and gas. [...] You can’t put the fire out while pouring petrol on it, and the Greens will fight Labor’s moves to expand coal and gas."

partyStatement.en: Coal and gas are the major causes of this climate crisis. Yet both major parties are backing more coal and gas. The Labor Government has approved over 25 coal and gas projects this term, and Dutton’s nuclear agenda is a distraction designed to delay action on the climate crisis. To keep people safe, we need to take real climate action by stopping new coal and gas, and investing in our communities so that everyone can withstand the climate crisis.

analystStatement.en: One Nation will apply a national plan that guarantees low-cost, reliable, dispatchable power by building new low-emission coal-fired power stations.
Australia is rich with natural resources. Our competitive advantage is in coal and gas. Pressing that advantage will make sure every Australian can benefit from the natural wealth of this nation.

Government spent $10.3 billion subsidising fossil fuels in 2020-21. We should not be subsidising or propping up stranded and failing industries. But it’s not only about taxpayers money, it’s about clear and consistent policy. Large corporations and investors are already redirecting funds away from fossil fuels to renewable energy and industries. Policy certainty will encourage this and grow our economy. Doing nothing will lead to an inevitable contraction as global demand for fossil fuels plummets and investors put their money elsewhere.

partyStatement.en: I don't want to see new fossil fuel projects approved and I support considering climate in our national environmental law. I have not previously supported a blanket ban because of the potential for a future scenario where this may be justified on national or economic security grounds for Australia or one of our close allies.

Australia's future lies in clean energy and technology, as it benefits from an increased competitive advantage through our abundance of renewable energy sources. The International Energy Agency has indicated that no new coal, oil or gas operations are consistent with limiting global warming. Whilst, there is recognition that certain operations will remain until 2050, expanding existing coal mining operations will lead to further emissions and acceleration of climate change impacts.
Coal is key to Australia's economic future.
I am unsure about this question as metallurgical coal is one of the components in the manufacturing of steel. We need to continue to make Australian steel.

label.en: How much should Australia do to reduce its carbon emissions?

analystStatement.en: The Opposition Leader [Peter Dutton] has said if he wins the next federal election, he would scrap Labor’s legislated target for 43 per cent emissions reduction by 2030 and focus on nuclear energy to reach net zero by 2050. The decision would place Australia at odds with its legally binding targets under the 2015 Paris Agreement, where nearly 200 countries committed to their own plans to reduce planet-warming emissions. [...] Mr Dutton in an interview with the Weekend Australian on Saturday argued there was “no sense” in ­signing up to the [2030] target which he claimed was unachievable.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition is committed to achieving net zero-emissions by 2050. But we will do this by considered planning that doesn't inflict higher power prices on the Australian economy and that doesn't result in manufacturing jobs moving offshore to countries with higher emissions than Australia. The Coalition has a plan to deliver a balanced energy mix, including zero-emissions nuclear which has been proven to get emissions down all over the world.

analystStatement.en: [T]he Albanese Government has introduced legislation to establish the Net Zero Economy Authority to ensure Australian workers and regions realise and share the benefits of the net zero economy. The Government is also announcing $189.3 million over four years from 2023-24 (and $53.3 million per year ongoing) in resourcing for the Authority. The Authority will support the economy-wide net zero transformation that is underway by acting as a catalyst for private and public investment, major project development, job creation and transition, and skills and community development. Global efforts to reduce emissions have already started transforming traditional industries, creating new opportunities to broaden Australia’s industrial base and strengthen our sovereign capability. The Albanese Government is already delivering a strong policy agenda to reduce emissions by 43 per cent on 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero by 2050.

partyStatement.en: After a decade of inaction, the Albanese Government has set ambitious emissions targets in law - net zero by 2050 and a 43% reduction on 2005 levels by 2030. According to the independent Climate Change Authority, Australia is on track to meet our 2030 target. We are also more than halfway towards reaching our target of 82% renewable energy in the national grid by 2030. We will set robust and responsible 2035 emission reductions targets based on CCA advice, keeping Australia on track for net zero by 2050. Key policy frameworks delivered since 2030 - including the Safeguard Mechanism and National Vehicle Emissions Standards - will help drive more carbon emissions reduction over time.

analystStatement.en: A nationwide, systematic response is required to drastically reduce emissions from all sectors, draw down greenhouse gases, and be greenhouse gas neutral or negative by 2035.

partyStatement.en: The Greens are fighting to: Stop new coal and gas; Expand publicly-owned renewable energy; End the billions in handouts to coal, oil and gas corporations; Lower power bills by transitioning to more reliable clean energy; Support households & businesses to electrify; Create thousands of jobs during the transition.

analystStatement.en: We strongly oppose the Liberals/Nationals' adoption of net-zero emissions targets and their costly green energy policies, which hurt Australian families and industries. Like Trump, we advocate for energy independence through the responsible use of Australia’s vast natural resources, including coal and gas. We reject the Paris Agreement as an undue burden on our economy.

Ambitious emissions reduction target by 2035 [...] Making significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions will not only help Australia to avoid the worst effects of climate change, but it will also safeguard our health, economic prosperity and national security for this and future generations.

partyStatement.en: It is in our economic interests, as well as in the interests of a liveable planet, to decarbonise our economy faster.

analystStatement.en: Climate change is among the most urgent and pressing challenges for Australia and the world. Strong action on climate change is a top priority.

partyStatement.en: I support the Climate Change Authority's position that 65-75% emissions target by 2035 is ambitious and achievable.
Australia lacks detailed plans about how each sector will decarbonise.

I support a 2035 target of up to 75% emissions reduction. The Climate Change Authority advises that a 65-75% target by then is ambitious and achievable. To reduce our emissions, it's critical we stay the course for 2030.

analystStatement.en: Beyond the Future Made in Australia policy, the budget outlines the government’s intention to continue to decarbonise the economy with the establishment of an independent Net Zero Economy Authority to co-ordinate Australia’s economic transition as well as sufficient agency funding to deliver its upcoming sector decarbonisation pathways. It’s good to see $155m for the New Vehicle Emissions Standards, including $60m for charging infrastructure. This will deliver more affordable EVs and the ongoing associated cost savings that Australians can enjoy. I also welcome the investment in our carbon credit market with $48m allocated to improve our carbon credits scheme and its integrity, something I have been advocating for in the last 12 months. Australia’s intention to host COP31 is also clearly evident with a $76.2m investment for international climate engagement. This will be an opportunity for Australia and highlights the shift Australia has made over the last few years on climate change policy but significantly more ambition is needed - starting with a commitment to a minimum of 75% emissions reduction by 2035 as our next nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement. Of great concern, Australia has been found to be consistently underreporting its methane emissions, and whilst this required only a $5.5m investment to ensure proper measurement and monitoring, there was nothing in the budget. It is disappointing that this funding was not prioritised given how critical it is that our emissions inventory has integrity to achieve the Government’s 43% emissions reduction target and commitments under the Paris Agreement.

partyStatement.en: Australia needs to transition to net zero as soon as possible to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. Climate risk is predicted to cost the Australian economy 14% of GDP annually by 2050. Carbon budgets are fast being exhausted to stay within safe temperature rises, so it is vital to have clear targets to drive investment, accelerate our transition with policy stability and keep our communities safe. I will continue to strongly advocate for Australia to commit to a 75% reduction in emissions by 2035.
We are killing off vital industries (and forcing others offshore) in pursuit of net zero. The measures put in place are unaffordable and unsustainable.

label.en: Australia should call for the immediate recognition of a Palestinian state.

analystStatement.en: [The Coalition] support[s] the idea of a two-state solution—a state of Israel and a state of Palestine living side by side. But the question is about the timing of the preconditions that need to exist before a Palestinian state should be recognised by Australia. The Australian foreign policy tradition is that we don't recognise states that haven't yet come into existence. [...] It's important that we don't recognise a state that hasn't come into existence, particularly when many of the actors in that state do not believe that Israel has a right to exist. That has always been a precondition for the recognition of a Palestinian state, in terms of Australian foreign policy.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition supports Australia's long-standing and previously bipartisan position in support of a negotiated two-state solution in which Israel and a future Palestinian coexist, in peace and security, within internationally recognised borders. “A two-state solution has to be one that comes about through negotiation. It needs security guarantees for both parties, it needs clear pathways to resolve the fundamentally difficult issues, like agreed borders and rights of return. Labor has supported motions which do not require negotiation and we are fundamentally opposed to that.”

analystStatement.en: Australia was among 143 UN general assembly members to pass the resolution calling on the security council to reconsider granting full membership to Palestine. On Saturday, [Minister for Foreign Affairs Penny] Wong said the vote was about awarding “modest additional rights to participate in United Nations forums”, and that Australia would only recognise Palestine “when we think the time is right”. She said Australia’s policy had changed to be open to recognition during a peace process, “not necessarily only at the end of the peace process”. [...] In a statement explaining the vote, the Australian government said the resolution’s language expressed “unwavering support for the two-state solution of Israel and Palestine, living side by side in peace and security within recognised borders”.

partyStatement.en: The Government supports a pathway to Palestinian self-determination and a two-state solution as essential to long-term peace and security in the region. The Government supports recognition of a Palestinian state as an integral part of that process.

analystStatement.en: [Adam Bandt]: "Recognition of Palestine is long overdue; 143 countries have already done it. Three more—Norway, Spain and Ireland—joined overnight, and today Australia must stand with them in recognising the state of Palestine. This is not just a symbolic move; it is a critical step towards peace and towards ending the slaughter that we are seeing with the invasion of Gaza right now."

partyStatement.en: The Australian Greens will continue to work for the Australian government to join the international community in recognising the statehood of Palestinians and maintain the position of not recognising Jerusalem as the capital of Israel.

analystStatement.en: In the Senate this week [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson asked the Labor government to ‘please explain’ why they supported an abhorrent and repugnant United Nations motion pushing full recognition of Palestine in their governing body. It was an outrageous move by Australia, and unmasked Labor’s nod to the domestic growth of antisemitic fever.

Russell Broadbent: "I stand with Israel, as this nation does. I stand, especially, knowing that there are Palestinians even in this country who wish for the end of the state of Israel. That is not going to happen. They have every right to respond to protect their border and to protect their people, and that's what they will do with all the force needed. [...] As we stand, Australia will do its best, and, I believe, the government will do its best to support wherever we need to support, whatever we can do. There will be humanitarian aid from this country for the peoples of Israel and the peoples of Palestine."

Kate Chaney (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

partyStatement.en: While I agree a two state solution is necessary, an immediate call by Australia is unlikely to contribute practically to this goal.

analystStatement.en: Zoe Daniel: "I strongly support Palestinian statehood under the auspices of a peace process leading to a two-state solution. In that, this moment is an opportunity for the Palestinian Authority, for example, to step up and show that it can reinvent itself to lead. To be clear, my concern is also for Israel and its people. A safe and secure future of the Israelis and the Palestinians is intertwined. Israel will not be truly safe until Palestine is also free. If only we could all have that clear-headed conversation about how we get there, rather than hurling abuse at each other inside and outside this chamber."

partyStatement.en: I support a Palestinian state, however currently there is no effective governance structure to implement it. A pathway to a 2 state solution requires the rebuilding of the Palestinian Authority, or a new body, to govern. Overnight declaration of a Palestinian state with no governance structure may be counter productive.

analystStatement.en: Andrew Gee: "Australia stands with the democracy of Israel and freedom-loving people everywhere. If these attacks were perpetrated against Australia, the public would demand a response. Israel has a right to defend itself and its citizens. We also need to remember and recognise that there are Palestinian people and Muslim communities around the world who are also appalled by this violence and terror and also wish for peace."

Helen Haines (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

partyStatement.en: I support a two-state solution and call on the government to take all steps possible towards peace and return of all remaining hostages.

analystStatement.en: Dai Le (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

Monique Ryan (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

Sophie Scamps (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

Allegra Spender: "Like many people in this room, I hope, I have always supported a two-state solution. [...] I have always dreamt, to be honest, of a situation where the Palestinian people and the Israeli people, the Jewish people, live side by side in self-determination and in separate states. [...] But what I am concerned about in this motion [to support the recognition of the State of Palestine] and in every motion that we have had on this issue in the House is that we are not actually achieving anything in terms of the difference it will make to the people in the conflict right now." [Ed. note: Allegra Spender voted no to the motion]

partyStatement.en: I support a 2 state solution in the Middle East. This must be negotiated between the two parties, not declared unilaterally by other countries.

analystStatement.en: Zali Steggall (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

partyStatement.en: Recognition of a Palestinan state should be part of a two-state solution in which Israel and a future Palestinian state coexist, in peace and security, within internationally recognised borders. The United States proposal to further displace Palestinian people from their land should be strongly rejected. According to the UN, such a proposal "would shatter fundamental rules of international order".

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "I do commend the government's reset on Jerusalem, but now we must also recognise Palestine, call for Israeli accountability in international courts and compel Israel to allow Palestinians to have the most basic of rights: self-determination."

Bob Katter (Katter's Australian Party) - No. Motion - Middle East - Recognise State of Palestine: “That this House endorses the Government’s position to support the recognition of the State of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace.” [3 July 2024]

partyStatement.en: I am concerned for the many civilians, particularly women and children who have been impacted by the war.
Australia should call for recognition of a Palestinian state only once there is a democratically elected Government presiding over Palestine as a whole.

label.en: Australia should deepen its ties with China.

analystStatement.en: When Peter Dutton was asked this week whether a Coalition government would continue to foster trade relations with China, he declared unequivocally that "the relationship with China will be much stronger than it is under the Albanese government". [...] Mid-last year Dutton said: "I'm pro-China and the relationship that we have with them. I want that trading relationship to increase … We need to make sure we strengthen the trading relationship because there are many businesses here who rely on it. But we have to be realistic about working to keep peace … we live in a very uncertain time.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition supports a stable and mutually respectful relationship with China: “We want to make sure that given China’s our biggest trading partner that we can continue to grow the relationship. We can be respectful, we want a strong relationship but as China is not going to compromise her national interest or her interests more generally, economically, nor should Australia be expected to."

analystStatement.en: [Prime Minister Anthony Albanese]: "As I've said many times, dialogue is crucial, and peace and stability take work. We recognise a more stable economic relationship between Australia and China is a good thing for workers, for businesses, for investors on both sides and for our countries more broadly. [Chinese] Premier Li, Australia has a vision of a peaceful, stable and prosperous world where sovereignty is respected and countries abide by international law. It's important that we have these frank exchanges of views on the issues that matter to us, to build deeper awareness of our respective interests."

partyStatement.en: Under the former Liberal government, Australia’s relations with China had deteriorated in all areas, including diplomatic engagement and trade. The Albanese Government has worked calmly and maturely to stabilise ties with our largest trading partner, without compromising on Australia’s national interest. The Albanese Government secured the resolution of all trade impediments that China had placed on $20 billion of Australian exports and saw Ms Cheng Lei reunited with her family. The Albanese government’s approach to China is to cooperate where we can, disagree where we must, and engage in the national interest.

analystStatement.en: [Australian Greens spokesperson for Foreign Affairs Jordon Steele-John]: “Improved relations between the People’s Republic of China and Australia will benefit both countries. [Chinese Premier Li's] visit is an opportunity to improve trade relationships, ensure peace within our region, and commit to taking urgent action on the climate crisis. [...] But, it is essential that Australia has a consistent approach to the condemnation of human rights abuses internationally.  It is paramount that the Prime Minister raise concerns of human rights abuses including Muslim minorities during Premier Li’s visit."

partyStatement.en: The Republic of China is Australia's largest trading partner and improved relations between the two countries will benefit our community, and maintain peace and stability in our region. The Greens believe Australia has a key role in maintaining peace in our region, including easing tensions between the United States and China. Additionally, the Greens have called on the Australian Government to raise concerns with the Chinese Government about human rights abuses, and have put forward a bill in the parliament to end the importation of goods produced by forced labor, including goods from places like Xinjiang.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "China is no friend of ours. We trade with them but [...] we trade with Coles and Woolworths. They're not our friends. China will never be our friends, and I'm sick of this Labor party, this Labor government kotowing to the Chinese every time [Prime Minister Anthony Albanese] opens his mouth."

partyStatement.en: A good trade and economic relationship with China is essential for Australia's economy.  We also have a long history of people-to-people links and an important Chinese-Australian community. We need to promote and deepen a positive trade relationship, while maintaining our core values and interests.

analystStatement.en: China remains Australia’s most significant trading partner and a profoundly important nation in the Indo-Pacific. Australia’s China policy should not be subject to partisan political point-scoring. Australia’s policy makers are, however, correct to be concerned about the increasing assertiveness of China’s diplomatic, military, and economic activity in the region. Australia must stake a position where it won’t be bullied but where it also won’t fight foreign policy battles on the front pages of the newspapers. We must finely balance our alliances in order that we can retain old friends, without isolating ourselves combatively from those who we must be able to converse with in our region. Diplomacy of the highest order is key at a time of great geopolitical upheaval.

partyStatement.en: Better a known known than a known unkown.

China is Australia's biggest trade partner. We have a very large Chinese-Australian population. We should strengthen our ties with all countries with which we have significant economic or diplomatic relationships.

analystStatement.en: Independent MP Allegra Spender says the government has made some “right moves” in its discussion with China following the meeting between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and China’s President Xi Jinping at the G20 in Bali. “I think what it has done is said very strongly 'these are the things that we find important' – it hasn’t backed down,” Ms Spender told Sky News Australia. “But it has held its position strongly but also restarted dialogue, and I think dialogue is absolutely crucial in foreign policy.”

partyStatement.en: A stable and constructive China-Australia relationship is in the interest of both countries. Australia should co-operate where it can, disagree where it must, and at all times, engage in Australia's national interest.

analystStatement.en: And yes, China in particular is increasingly belligerent and dealing with that is obviously challenging for Australia. But the solution is not to try and outgun them, or to continue to cuddle up to Washington and prepare for more expeditionary military operations with the US, including potentially against China. That will just inflame the situation and guarantee Australia stays on the Chinese target list. It is a significant failure of Australian foreign and security policy that governments think they must choose between the US and China. It was always the case we would be better off with a more independent foreign and security policy based on Australia’s national interest and the maintenance of good relations with both countries.

partyStatement.en: Australia is an important trading partner, however there are cultural considerations and political differences.

label.en: How much should Australia spend on its military?

analystStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition Government will make a significant investment in defence. We will equip our military at speed and scale to play our part as a credible partner in promoting peace through strength.

partyStatement.en: Australia is facing the most complex and serious strategic circumstances since the end of the Second World War. Only the Coalition is committed to backing Defence by increasing the current Defence budget and providing our ADF with the capabilities they need. The Coalition will provide an initial $3 billion of additional funding to Defence towards the acquisition of a fourth squadron of F-35A fighter aircraft. This will bolster the Royal Australian Air Force’s strike and air combat capabilities, adding some 28 aircraft to the current fleet of 72 to reach a total of 100 F-35As – the Coalition’s original commitment. This funding restores the allocation which the Albanese Government cut.

analystStatement.en: Australia's projected defence spending will increase by another $50 billion over the next decade, with the government unveiling an immediate boost of more than $1 billion to accelerate long-range missiles and targeting systems, as well as lethal autonomous systems. Defence Minister Richard Marles has released Labor's long-awaited National Defence Strategy, which aims to put Australia's total defence spending at 2.4 per cent of GDP within 10 years. Total government defence investment in the military is expected to reach $330 billion through to 2033-34, which includes initial costs for the massive AUKUS initiative to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government will continue to ensure our defence forces, security agencies, police and emergency services are always appropriately resourced and given the necessary powers to respond to defend Australia’s sovereignty and protect our national interests. We are making record investments in Defence, including an additional $5.7 billion over the next four years and $50.3 billion over the next decade.

analystStatement.en: The Albanese [Government] has announced a staggering $330 billion spend on Defence over the next decade, the vast majority going into the same white elephant projects such as nuclear submarines and (very) future frigates that have been burning through public funds for years. [...] “This latest review fails to deal with the giant AUKUS-sized-elephant in the room that has eaten up Defence’s budget and imposed the extra cost of less stability and the peace in the region. [...] This is a major missed opportunity to refocus our defence spending to a much more affordable, less aggressive and more achievable direction that is aimed at defending Australia rather than threatening our neighbours,” [Greens Defence Spokesperson David Shoebridge] said.

partyStatement.en: Withdrawing from the AUKUS political pact would save $73 billion over the next ten years. This could be reinvested in programs like seeing the GP for free, dental and mental health into medicare and more public and affordable housing.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "We have a massive commitment to the new AUKUS alliance. Those nuclear subs are not going to be cheap, but I support them."
I am concerned about the very high cost of upgrading our defence to include nuclear submarines. Like so many people, I have wondered how $368 billion might be otherwise spent in Australia.

partyStatement.en: The global geopolitical landscape is changing and we need to ensure we are protecting our national interests.

analystStatement.en: The security and safety of the Australian people is the paramount responsibility of Government. Defence spending should be commensurate with the geopolitical and regional circumstances in which Australia finds itself. Clearly, the world and the Indo-Pacific are less secure than they were a decade ago. Spending on defence needs to recognise these circumstances and predict future challenges. This is not, however, a matter of spending for spending’s sake. Financial commitments have been made, but ineffective decision making means that Australia will be less protected than would otherwise have been the case (especially in relation to a new generation of submarines) during a period of heightened tension and risk. This needs urgent correction. Our circumstances also suggest the need for greater emphasis on diplomacy (including soft diplomacy) rather than merely militarising our international relations.

Andrew Gee: "The new AUKUS partnership [with the UK and the US] is a watershed, momentous announcement in terms of our alliance partnerships. The announcement on the nuclear propelled submarines is also equally momentous."

Dai Le [Independent]: "The government has committed to spending $368 billion on acquiring nuclear powered submarines when people are struggling to pay the grocery bills, yet we still don't know the full cost to taxpayers and where and how the nuclear waste will be stored. What will it cost our taxpayers to manage this nuclear waste, and will Australia be accepting any nuclear waste from other AUKUS countries under the agreement?"

Given the uncertain geopolitical environment, I believe some investments to upgrade and maintain our military capability are required. The bi-partisan AUKUS program represents the largest such investment into Australia’s defence force capability in recent decades, however, I acknowledge the concerns held by many in my community regarding the total cost of the AUKUS program, the lack of transparency around it, and defence spending more generally. I support the intent of the AUKUS program but believe we must continually scrutinise the timelines, costs and expected strategic benefits of such programs over the long-term. In my capacity as an independent member of parliament, I regularly meet with, and receive briefings from, the Deputy Prime Minister and Defence leadership to do just that.

partyStatement.en: With the uncertainty of the current geopolitical environment some significant investments in defence are required.

Our spending on military needs to reflect the complex strategic environment that Australia currently sits. This might be higher than current spending of 2% of GDP, but greater scrutiny and accountability of defence spending is needed with clear KPIs for deliverables.
Australia needs an effective defence force which means we should spend our existing budget much more effectively, and definitely not on nuclear submarines.

analystStatement.en: If, all goes to plan, by sometime in the mid-2040s - Australian may have a total of 26 warships to protect one of the biggest coastlines on earth. [...] AUSTRALIAN Defence’s culture needs to be examined as much as its ageing and underwhelming equipment Katter’s Australian Party MP Bob Katter says, who has proposed “accountants in Cairns,” Far North Queensland could prop up Navy numbers in response to concerns of “weak borders”. Responding to reports a new fleet of “smaller” warships are set to be announced by the Federal Government after its strategic review found the Navy had “a lack of firepower” and “not enough crew,” Mr Katter said Defence’s leadership also needed to be scrutinised for dwindling personnel retention.

partyStatement.en: Funding needs to be directed to northern Australia. We need a missile fortress wall and a defence force that is capable of defending Australia from a threat (including combat ready naval fleet).

label.en: Australia should cut its ties to the monarchy.

analystStatement.en: [Opposition Leader Peter Dutton]: "Through times of peace and war, constitutional and parliamentary crises, good times and bad, Australians have known stability and have taken confidence knowing that there are better days ahead because our institutions are protected and underpinned by the independence and stoicism of the reigning Monarch."

partyStatement.en: The Coalition believes Australia has benefited from the stability of a democracy with the monarchy as our bedrock. While this is ultimately a consideration for the Australian people via a referendum, we believe the current constitutional arrangements have served us well since Federation.

analystStatement.en: It is a longstanding policy of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to hold a referendum on becoming a republic. But a minister has told local media that such a vote is "not a priority" and there is "no timeline" for it. [...] Pressed further on the topic on ABC on Monday, Assistant Minister for the Republic Matt Thistlethwaite said there was "no timeline". He instead highlighted the need to tackle cost-of-living issues. [...] But Mr Thistlethwaite said he was "not giving up", and it was still the plan of the governing Labor Party for Australia to break away from the UK Royal Family "longer term".

partyStatement.en: Holding a referendum on becoming a republic is not a priority right now and there is no timeline for it.

analystStatement.en: Australia values democracy, fairness, and independence. The British monarchy no longer reflects who we are, or the future we want to build. [...] The Greens are working to deliver a democratic consultative process to ensure the public shapes the future of Australia as a republic.

partyStatement.en: Australia deserves a democratic head of state that reflects our values and independence, not inherited from a colonial monarchy. Becoming a republic is about taking pride in our identity, maturing as a nation, and standing on our own as a fully independent and democratic country.

analystStatement.en: [Monarchist League's national chair Philip Benwell] described [Katherine] Deves and [One Nation Leader Pauline] Hanson as “staunch monarchists”.

partyStatement.en: Personally agree but this is a matter for the Australian people at a referendum.
I support a referendum to decide if Australia should become a republic, but in being a republic it does not mean we cut all ties with the monarchy.

analystStatement.en: Allegra Spender: "As the Prime Minister said this morning, 'You could be a republican and still have a deep affection and respect for [Queen Elizabeth II].' I think people in all walks of life, certainly in Wentworth, acknowledge the stability that her reign has provided our own democracy, even as many consider how our democracy may change."

partyStatement.en: Personally, I support Australia becoming a republic, but this is a decision for the entire population via referendum.
As a modern, multicultural nation, Australia should have an Australian head of state. However, this needs to be decided by the people through a referendum.

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "It strikes me as an anachronism that the Queen of England is also the Queen of Australia and that our parliament is opened by her representative in this country. Surely we have grown up and moved on. I have fond feelings towards our mother country and what England did to settle us, help us grow and become a great nation. But, surely, now, 226 years after the First Fleet sailed into Port Jackson, it is beyond time that we had an Australian head of state and an Australian open this parliament."

Bob Katter: "Everyone who comes to this place swears allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, with one exception. I didn't, and I never have. In my 51 years in politics I've refused to swear allegiance to a foreign monarch. I'm an Australian."

partyStatement.en: But retain the Westminster system of government and celebrate our own national heroes. Allegiance should be to Australia first.

label.en: How much of a role should the private sector have in health care?

analystStatement.en: Health insurance premiums will rise by an average of 3.73 per cent from April after lengthy negotiations between the federal government and insurers, with the opposition describing the hike as "another hit" to Australian household budgets. [...] Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston said the rise was the highest premium increase in seven years. "It is another hit to Australians' household budgets at a time when they can least afford it,"  she said. "The Albanese government has hidden this cost hike from them for months, leaving Australians with private health insurance minimal time to prepare their budgets and shop around."

partyStatement.en: The Coalition will support Australians to receive healthcare in a timely way wherever they live.
