We have committed $9 billion to Medicare, to address the crisis in our primary health system, in addition to $1.7 billion for public hospitals for the next financial year. This demonstrates our absolute support for Medicare, together with a strong public health system, while also valuing the contribution made to healthcare in Australia by a strong and viable non-government hospital and health insurance sector.

analystStatement.en: Labor recognises that both public and private sectors play critical roles in Australia’s world-class health system. Labor is committed to ensuring that private health insurance delivers value for Australians and that the costs of health are borne fairly by all Australians.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government believes in universal access to world class public health care. Labor recognises that both public and private sectors play critical roles in Australia’s world-class health system. Labor is committed to ensuring that private health insurance delivers value for Australians and that the costs of health are borne fairly by all Australians.

analystStatement.en: Liberal and Labor undermined the public health system by pushing people into a private health insurance industry run for profit, not people. The public pays $7 billion to the Private Health Insurance industry each year - making care cheaper for the rich, while people who can’t afford private health insurance face long waiting lists. The Greens will make dental and mental health care part of medicare, and reinvest the private health rebate back into the public system so we can slash wait times and remove out of pocket costs.

partyStatement.en: In a wealthy country like ours, everyone should have access to the healthcare they need. Too many people are unable to access affordable healthcare and are experiencing long wait times. Right now people are delaying seeing their GP because of the cost, they are struggling to access mental health services, and can not afford the dental care they require. The Greens are prioritising funding a world-class public health system, investing in public hospitals, building free local healthcare centres across the country, and expanding Medicare including getting dental into Medicare. Right now, 1 in 3 big corporations pay no tax. By making big corporations pay their fair share, we can expand Medicare, reduce out-of-pocket costs, and ensure all Australians have access to the healthcare services they deserve.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "We expect people to fund their own health insurance, so they have to pay for their education."

Russell Broadbent: "So we still ask people to make a contribution, and what the Australian government is doing through this legislation is trying to make it easier and more affordable for Australians to have that confidence of being able to buy and support themselves through private health insurance. On the other hand, we're asking the private health insurers to make a contribution to the nation, as well, by streamlining the services they have and finding ways to reduce costs. We're keeping the pressure on the private health insurers to make sure they're delivering the best service that they can, from the premiums that they are given, for real value for the Australian people."

Affordable, accessible medical care is not just a human right, but an investment in our population that pays enormous dividends. [...] Much is made of the cost of publicly funded healthcare, but there is no economy without a healthy community. Having seen the disastrous and inequitable health system in the United States close up, I see Australia’s health care system as fundamental to the strength of our nation.
Helen Haines (Independent) - Aye. Motion - Private Health Insurance Amendment (Income Thresholds) Bill 2021 - Second readings: “That the bill be now read a second time.” [1 June 2021]

Sophie Scamps: "I rise today to express my deep concern at the state of public healthcare services in my electorate of Mackellar, on the northern beaches of Sydney. Over the last decade, Mackellar has seen our public hospital placed under the management of a private company in a public-private partnership arrangement, the withdrawal of drug and alcohol rehabilitation and the withdrawal of public dental services, a critical lack of both local hospital and community-based mental health services, a paucity of specialist medical outpatient services and a shortage of healthcare workers. The northern beaches have a population almost the same size as Canberra, yet we only have half a public hospital run by a private provider."

partyStatement.en: A strong Australia is a place where everyone feels safe and supported regardless of age, race, religious belief, gender and ability. In doing so, the Australian government should ensure that all Australians have access to high-quality healthcare.

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "[W]e need immediate and extensive reform of the private health insurance industry not just to prevent the industry's collapse but also to protect consumers and to ensure independent health service providers, like optometrists, dentists and others, can enjoy a genuinely sustainable future."

partyStatement.en: To make healthcare affordable and accessible to all, private health care is a key ingredient.

label.en: How accessible should abortion services be in Australia?

analystStatement.en: Neither Labor nor the Coalition have plans to change the status quo when it comes to abortion, which is legal in all Australian jurisdictions, with both parties insisting that it is an issue for the states. [...] Asked about his personal views on the matter, the opposition leader said he supported "a woman's right to choose".

partyStatement.en: The Coalition supports the current arrangements and is not proposing any changes on this issue. The delivery of specific pregnancy termination services is a state and territory responsibility and the Australian Government has no constitutional powers in this area.  The laws relating to pregnancy termination vary by jurisdiction.

analystStatement.en: Neither Labor nor the Coalition have plans to change the status quo when it comes to abortion, which is legal in all Australian jurisdictions, with both parties insisting that it is an issue for the states. [...] In 2019, while in opposition, Labor promised that if re-elected they would make the federal funding the government allocates to major public hospitals conditional on them providing abortion services. It later dumped the policy and now takes the position that abortion is a matter for the states and territories. "That's not our policy and I don't have any intention to revisit it," Health Minister Mark Butler told reporters on Wednesday.

partyStatement.en: The Commonwealth is responsible for medical termination, as we oversee the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme. The Albanese Government, has increased access to MS-2 Step© by removing several restrictions on health professionals who prescribe and dispense MS-2 Step. This has improved women's access to medical terminations. In the year since those changes, close to three times as many GPs have prescribed, and more than twice as many pharmacies have dispensed MS-2 Step for the first time. Access to medical abortions has greatly improved, with women now able to get the support they need from their regular GP and pharmacist. Because of these changes, more women have more choice and access to medical abortions. Surgical abortions are a state and territory responsibility, because they run public hospitals.

analystStatement.en: The Greens will provide $100m a year to ensure all public hospitals provide abortion services, moving the conversation from legality to affordability and accessibility. [...] Greens leader in the Senate and spokesperson on Women, Larissa Waters [said:] "Reproductive healthcare must not be a culture war or a postcode lottery. No one should fall through the cracks when it comes to accessing vital healthcare. While abortion is now legal across the country, whether or not you can actually access this time-bound healthcare is a postcode lottery."

partyStatement.en: Reproductive healthcare must not be a culture war or a postcode lottery. No one should fall through the cracks when it comes to accessing vital healthcare. While abortion is now legal across the country, whether or not you can actually access this time-bound healthcare is a postcode lottery. With the closure of many private abortion facilities in recent years, many women - particularly those in regional and remote areas - are left with little choice but to travel hundreds of kilometres and spend thousands of dollars. The Greens will provide $100m per year to equip public hospitals with the personnel and facilities required to provide terminations services.

analystStatement.en: One Nation will: Reduce the gestational limit for abortions; [...] Ban sex-selective abortion; [...] Restore Doctor’s Rights [...] to a full conscientious objection to abortion.

I believe that women need to be able to access abortion safely and equitably.  In one of my first speeches as a newly sworn-in member of Parliament I spoke about the need for equal access to abortion for all women: Harmonisation of abortion laws across Australia is overdue. [...] We need to remain vigilant and ensure there is equal and free access, with abortion incorporated into normal healthcare systems.

partyStatement.en: I support harmonisation across the States on the approach to abortion to ensure there is equal and free access, with abortion incorporated into normal healthcare systems

analystStatement.en: I was asked if abortion was coming back as an issue in our politics [...] My response was simple. Get your hands off women’s bodies. Women are able to make their own choices and deserve to be given that fundamental human right. Abortion should not be a political issue.

Helen Haines: "A recent study by Women’s Health Victoria showed the postcode lottery of sexual and reproductive health access across the state and it showed service deserts, where 67 per cent of local government areas did not have any listed surgical abortion providers, 45 per cent did not have any listed medical abortion providers and 60 per cent did not have any listed medication abortion dispensing pharmacies. In mid 2023, just 17 per cent of GPs were providing medication abortion services. Could you imagine a men’s health issue where more than 80 per cent of GPs did not offer treatment? It simply would not happen."

partyStatement.en: As a nurse and midwife, I know how important it is that we have equitable access in regional and rural areas where services are lacking.

analystStatement.en: Monique Ryan: Excellent to see the government making reproductive choices easier and more affordable for all Australian women. This is well overdue.
Dr [Sophie] Scamps: "I also want to recognise [...] the recent historic introduction in New South Wales of positive consent legislation and the decriminalising of abortion."

partyStatement.en: There have been recent examples of regional hospitals in NSW cutting or limiting these services.

analystStatement.en: [Allegra Spender]: "Women and girls need access to safe and legal abortions - they need control over their bodies. This change in the USA is terrible and around the world we must guard our hard-fought rights. #RoeVsWade"
Independent Warringah MP Zali Steggall said she strongly supported making abortion more affordable and available and would be happy to discuss the issue with government MPs.

partyStatement.en: A strong Australia is a place where everyone feels safe and supported regardless of age, race, religious belief, gender and ability. In doing so, the Australian government should ensure that all Australians have access to high-quality healthcare, including access to abortion care.

analystStatement.en: Katter’s Australian Party (KAP) MPs will vehemently oppose any expansion of access to abortion across Queensland.

partyStatement.en: Abortion services are not a Federal Government issue, legislation sits with states and territories.

label.en: The Australian government should pay the full cost of family doctor visits.

analystStatement.en: The Coalition has vowed to match Labor's pledge to boost Medicare funding by $8.5 billion "dollar-for-dollar", as the government moved to set up a federal election contest fought on access to health care. Labor has promised nine out of 10 GP visits will be free from out-of-pocket expenses by the end of the decade, in what will be a cornerstone of their re-election pitch to voters struggling with the cost of living.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition will make visits to a family doctor more affordable with an historic $8.5 billion investment to deliver better access to a GP, more free visits and more doctors and nurses across Australia. As part of our historic primary healthcare package, the Coalition will expand the Medicare bulk billing incentive to all Australians and provide significant support to GPs to offer bulk billed services to the community. These measures are projected to restore GP bulk billing back up to the record-high levels reached under the former Coalition Government, meaning more Australians will be able to access their doctor for free. It is anticipated that these measures will see 90% of GP visits being bulk billed by 2030, up from 77% currently under Labor, which has overseen an 11% drop since in government.

analystStatement.en: Labor has promised nine out of 10 GP visits will be free from out-of-pocket expenses by the end of the decade, in what will be a cornerstone of their re-election pitch to voters struggling with the cost of living. The policy expands the bulk billing incentive to all Australians and includes a bonus for doctors who bulk-bill all patients at a cost of $8.5 billion over four years.

partyStatement.en: From 1 November 2025, for the first time, the Australian Government will expand GP bulk billing incentives to all Medicare-eligible people and create an additional new incentive payment for practices that bulk bill every patient. The combined investment means approximately 4,800 practices will be in a better financial position if they adopt full bulk billing – meaning they will receive more in Medicare payments than they currently receive in patient fees. At these 4,800 practices, visits to the family doctor will be fully covered by the Australian Government. Currently, a bulk billing GP earns less than their mixed billing or privately billing colleagues for providing the same number of services. The government's investment fixes that by increasing the financial reward a GP receives when they bulk bill, closing the gap between a fully bulk billing GP and a mixed billing GP. This investment boosts Medicare payments for all sorts of GP visits, including long consultations and mental health consults by applying the bulk billing incentive to these items for all Australians, for the first time ever.

analystStatement.en: [T]he Greens will [...] Support a return to bulk-billed GP appointments, by tripling the bulk-billing incentive for all people with a Medicare card.; Establish 1,000 free healthcare clinics, allowing people to access a GP, dentist, registered nurse or psychologist with no out-of-pocket costs.

partyStatement.en: With bulk-billing options plummeting across the country and millions of people delaying healthcare due to cost concerns, the Greens have announced an ambitious plan to enable all Australians to go to the GP for free. The Greens plan includes increasing bulk-billing incentive payments for everyone with a Medicare, increasing Medicare rebates for longer appointments, and establishing 6 free local healthcare clinics in every electorate where people can see a GP, nurse practitioner, dentist or psychologist for free. The plan will be paid for by taxing big corporations so that they pay their fair share of tax.

analystStatement.en: One Nation is committed to strengthening Medicare by cracking down on fraud and ensuring funds are directed toward improving bulk-billing rates and reducing out-of-pocket costs for Australians. [...] One Nation will [...] Increase Medicare rebates to ensure GPs are properly remunerated, encouraging more bulk-billing and reducing costs for patients.

Russell Broadbent: "The services that are provided when people can't get in to see a GP now or [...] have to move from a bulk-billing to fee-paying clinical centre—these are all issues affecting families that can least afford this. They need to be able to get to a bulk-billing [e.g. government-funded] centre."

partyStatement.en: All Australians should have access to a GP.

analystStatement.en: Zoe Daniel: As an aside, having lived in the US where lives are routinely ruined due to the cost of basic healthcare I will never support the dismantling or erosion of Medicare and our public health system. Not negotiable. Good health and a strong economy go together btw

partyStatement.en: Preventative health care is cheaper for the public purse in the long run.

analystStatement.en: Helen Haines: "In regional Victoria we have a higher than average chronic burden of disease. If we need to see a doctor in Indi, only 12 of our 33 GP practices bulk-bill, and the bulk-billing rate is only 18 per cent, according to research by Cleanbill. So the incentives announced in the budget by the government to increase the amount of bulk-billing by GPs are extremely welcome. I really hope that they do work for the people of Indi, because this is a major cost and a major contributor to the lack of access to GPs and to the chronic disease burden that we experience."

partyStatement.en: Our medicare rebate system needs reform to ensure the sustainability of General Practice.

analystStatement.en: With more and more GPs now having to turn away from bulk-billing, basic healthcare services are becoming less affordable for pensioners. The first point of contact with a health issue is now becoming less accessible. GPs in my area who still choose to bulk-bill are being so inundated with patients that locals have to wait weeks just to see them. The Australian Medical Association have told me that some of their doctors are at the point where they must stop bulk-billing in order to run a financially sustainable medical centre, but they refuse to do so as many of their elderly patients would opt to avoid seeing the doctor altogether if they needed to pay out-of-pocket costs.

[Monique Ryan]: "The fundamental principles of the Medicare system are true to what the Australian people want, need and deserve: universality, shared Commonwealth and state responsibility for public hospital care and a universal insurance against medical costs, including via bulk billing."

Dr [Sophie] Scamps: "[T]he government's injection of $3.5 billion to triple the incentive payments for GPs to bulk-bill children, pensioners and concession card holders is a crucial health equity measure and will provide cost-of-living relief."

Ms [Allegra] Spender: "One of the issues my community of Wentworth have raised with me is access to bulk-billing appointments with local GPs about prices rising and clinics closing. So I was pleased to see the government triple the bulk-billing incentives for GPs. I think that's absolutely critical. This will go a long way to ensuring that there are more bulk-billed appointments available and that we don't lose more GPs from our area."

partyStatement.en: I want to see bulk billing available to more people when they need it.
All Australians should have access to affordable, high-quality healthcare. Bulk billing and Medicare rebate should be available equitably across all health services providers.

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "It is an undeniable fact that many Australians simply can't find a GP with open books—or, at least, one that might bulk-bill. It's an undeniable fact that hospital emergency departments are heavily populated with non-emergency patients. It's an undeniable fact that many Australians are financially stretched to breaking point right now, and the big and growing gap fees are just one more pressure on those family budgets. [...] I call on the government to have a better set of priorities and to invest more money in general practice."

partyStatement.en: Medical care should not depend on the size of your wallet, yet we need to ensure that the system isn't abused.

analystStatement.en: Rebekha Sharkie: "I’m calling it a ‘meat and potatoes’ Federal Budget - it’s basic but filling. Positives: [...] Tripling Medicare bulk billing incentive will hopefully see Drs return to bulk billing children & health card holders."

partyStatement.en: Access to primary health care is critically important and those who cannot afford to pay a gap should not be excluded from access to health care. Children and those with a Commonwealth Health Care card should be bulk billed wherever possible.

label.en: There should be a limit on how much landlords can raise the rent they charge tenants.

analystStatement.en: A rent freeze has been part of the national housing conversation since it was proposed by Australian Greens housing spokesperson Max Chandler-Mather in 2022. [...] Liberal housing spokesperson Michael Sukkar panned the rent freeze proposal. “It would definitely lead to less rental stock being available and less rental stock ever being built in the future,” he said in a statement.

partyStatement.en: Tenancy law is primarily a responsbility of the states and territories. A national rent freeze would lead to less rental stock being available and less rental stock ever being built in the future.

analystStatement.en: Move towards a national standard of no more than one rent increase per year for a tenant in the same property across fixed and ongoing agreements.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government believes landlords should not be able to increase rents more than once per year - and this is in our national Better Deal for Renters. Labor does not believe in rent caps or freezing rents as the evidence shows this will make matters worse for renters - supply falls and renters are treated worse.

analystStatement.en: Millions of renters are struggling to keep a roof over their head, while the Labor Government continues to hand billions in tax handouts to wealthy property investors. People need relief right now. That's why the Greens are fighting for: An immediate rent freeze for 2 years coordinated through National Cabinet; Following the freeze, capping future rental increases at 2% every 2 years.

partyStatement.en: Renters know the system has been stacked against them. It’s designed by wealthy property investors, for wealthy property investors. This is why the Greens have a plan to establish a National Renters Protection Authority that’s in the corner of renters – ready to fight for them. Under our plan, the NRPA will have the power to: Independently investigate breaches of rental law; Fine individual landlords up to $15,650 or real estate agents up to $78,250 for breaching renters rights; Offer advocacy, advice and education to renters across the country. The NRPA would play a key role in enforcing new national tenancy standards. The Greens’ plan would distribute $2.5 billion each year to the states and territories that adopt new model rental laws. Those include freezing and capping rent increases, access to 5-year leases, a guaranteed right to lease renewal, and stronger minimum standards for heating, cooling, insulation and ventilation.

analystStatement.en: Malcolm Roberts [One Nation Acting Whip]: "Rent is certainly an issue for Queenslanders. Listening across regional Queensland in recent weeks, what I heard most about rent controls was how much damage they do. A rent cap damages before it's introduced. The Greens announced they're pursuing rent caps, and landlords all over the country are now furiously putting up rents ready for the freeze. New homes are being let at higher rents for the same reason. Lease terms are being shortened so landlords will not be trapped in a lease that causes them a financial loss."

Russell Broadbent: "Why do we have a rental crisis? Because state government policies are good for the renter and they establish the rights of the person renting the house. I grew up with 'caveat emptor'—let the buyer beware. Let the Australian people make their own decisions on their own behalf. If you don't want to rent at that price, don't rent at that price. Rentals are being taken off the market, and that is being caused by government policy and only government policy."
Kate Chaney: "It's broadly accepted that the current housing problem is a supply problem and needs to be addressed with supply levers."

partyStatement.en: While we need stronger renter protections, if appropriate incentives are in place to drive adequate housing supply, this type of market intervention wouldn't be necessary.

analystStatement.en: My ideas around affordable housing go to the kinds of innovative rent to buy and discounted rent schemes that are taking off overseas and I think they can fit the above concepts with some strong thought leadership and planning. While I do not support alterations to negative gearing, if elected, I will strongly advocate for expert review into affordable housing and rental accommodation, including an increase to rental assistance that ensures it keeps pace with the CPI.

partyStatement.en: Agree with renters rights and European style long leases but evidence suggests rent controls don't work and may reduce private investment to the extent that demand-supply issues emerge.

analystStatement.en: Dr [Sophie] Scamps: "We hear countless stories of the lack of renters' rights and of renters who face eviction in the face of unaffordable rent hikes or who have to move home frequently."

Ms [Allegra] Spender: "In August, National Cabinet committed to strengthening renters' rights by ending no-grounds evictions, limiting rent increases to once a year and phasing in minimum rental standards. But, three months on, not enough has changed. Renters are facing the highest rent increases since 2009, there are continued no-grounds evictions, and there are rising power bills because of poor home energy performance. When will the commitments made by National Cabinet be implemented across all states and territories, and will this include ending no-cause evictions at the end of a fixed term?"

partyStatement.en: I support stronger protections for renters and longer term leases but the evidence is that strict rent controls don't work.
Access to safe housing is an essential human right. All Australians should have access to safe, affordable and quality housing. Yearly rent increases should be regulated and capped.

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "My question is to the housing minister. Minister, in 2023, National Cabinet agreed on nine reforms under A Better Deal for Renters. However, both the national shelter and the tenants union note that in Tasmania the state government is currently not pursuing six of the nine agreed reforms. Why is the Tasmanian government being allowed to slow-walk these agreed reforms, and will the federal government finally inject some urgency into nationally consistent protections for renters?"

In October 2021, the Palaszczuk Government passed Stage 1 of the rental law reforms which introduced a swag of tenant protections. The most significant of the changes included ending without grounds evictions, strengthening renter protections against eviction and rent increases, allowing more renters to have pets and allowing renters experiencing domestic and family violence the right to end their interest in a tenancy without liability for costs. The last of the Stage 1 reforms will be implemented in September 2024. [...] Hinchinbrook MP and KAP Deputy Leader, Nick Dametto said the Government had simply missed the mark when it came to alleviating pressure in the housing and rental markets.

partyStatement.en: Renting caps should not be present just to allow people to survive in the cities. Measures should be put in place for families to thrive in the regions.

label.en: Boats carrying asylum seekers should be turned back.

analystStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition will [...] Build on the success of Operation Sovereign Borders to expand and enhance our border security to stop people smuggling and secure our borders.

partyStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition Government will build on the success of Operation Sovereign Borders to expand and enhance our border security to stop people smuggling and secure our borders. The Coalition is strongly committed to turnbacks where it is safe to do so - these formed an important part of the former Coalition Government’s successful border protection policy Operation Sovereign Borders (OSB).  The three pillars of OSB – Temporary Protection Visas, Regional Processing and turnbacks where it is safe to do so –  successfully halted the people smugglers, stopped the deaths at sea and removed all the children from detention.

analystStatement.en: [Former] Home Affairs Minister Clare O'Neil said funding for Operation Sovereign Borders had never been higher. [...] "If you attempt an illegal boat journey to Australia you will either be turned back or sent to Nauru," Ms O'Neil said.

partyStatement.en: Australia’s Operation Sovereign Borders policy architecture remains unchanged. Anyone who attempts an unauthorised boat voyage to Australia will be turned back to their point of departure, returned to their home country or transferred to another country.

analystStatement.en: The Australian Greens believe that: [...] Seeking asylum is a human right. People who enter Australian territory to seek asylum do so lawfully. Asylum seeking is a humanitarian issue rather than an issue of border security or defence, and people seeking asylum must be treated with compassion, as our equal in rights and dignity.

partyStatement.en: Under the policies of the Liberals and Labor, our immigration system has become cruel and dysfunctional, prioritising borders and economics over people and communities. The Greens are committed to rebuilding an immigration system that reflects these core Australian values—welcoming refugees with dignity, supporting families with fairness, and fostering social inclusion. We are working to deliver a system that strengthens our communities, upholds human rights, and collaborates with our region to create lasting, cooperative solutions for those seeking safety and a new life.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "Australia must return to the full model that stopped the boats. It's the only proven effective model that prevents deaths at sea. It's a model admired in many countries whose borders are being attacked by people smugglers."

partyStatement.en: Australia should take asylum seekers through appropriate channels and treat people with compassion, but must be careful not to create incentives for people smugglers.

analystStatement.en: Zoe Daniel: "If the government plans to stick with its plan not to permanently resettle people in Australia who come by boat—I don't agree with it—what is the plan?"

partyStatement.en: Having covered the deaths of asylum seekers who have come by boat as a reporter I have major safety concerns for those who attempt to reach Australia by boat.

analystStatement.en: Helen Haines: "Australians want a nation that has control of its sea borders but does not leave desperate people to languish indefinitely in prisons. The Asia-Pacific asylum seeker solution does both of these things at once by creating a network of centres across the region. People no longer have an incentive to risk their lives on boats. By enabling people to apply at these centres we have a single, virtual queue where we are completely in control over who is granted asylum to this country."

Dai Le [Independent]: "I agree with the government's stance that we need to make sure that those who enter our country are legitimate refugees, and that we do not encourage people smugglers who are profiteering off desperate people. [...] I support some form of processing, but in a fair way, because we do need to ensure genuine refugees can get the opportunity to be resettled."

[Monique Ryan]: "[T]he people of Kooyong [...] have sent me to represent Kooyong's call for humane treatment of refugees and people seeking asylum. I heard that call from the people of Kooyong almost every day as I sought their support to become their member during the recent election. Many of the volunteers who generously gave their time to the campaign are about as passionate as you can get about the rights of refugees and asylum seekers."

Dr [Sophie] Scamps: "My community in Mackellar, like many communities around Australia, is showing the way when it comes to proving we do not need to be cruel when it comes to the treatment of refugees. I believe my community is showing the true spirit of the Australian soul."

I'm focussed on [...] Compassionate treatment of refugees – including ending the uncertainty for eight thousand asylum seekers living in limbo for a decade, introducing a 90-day limit on detention, and banning detention of children.

Zali Steggall: "It is time to be brave and generous. That is not what we've got here. We make a mockery of our national anthem every time we extend offshore detention processing and refugee policies. We sing, 'For those who come across the seas, we've boundless plains to share,' yet your policy is that, if you come across the sea, you will be turned back and sent somewhere else. So we make a mockery of our Australian anthem."

partyStatement.en: Australian immigration and asylum seeker policies must be consistent with international human rights law and be consistent regardless of how asylum seekers reach Australia by boat or by plane. Australia has an obligation to treat asylum seekers and refugees humanely and fairly, whilst maintaining strong border protection and developing greater cooperation and prevention within our region.

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "The government would say, the minister would say, that the current regime of Operation Sovereign Borders and offshore processing works and has stopped the boats. But the end does not justify the means, in particular when there are other approaches we should be considering and exploring. Four months ago there was an opportunity for us to come into this place and debate and explore the possibility of other responses to irregular immigrants, to ask ourselves, 'Are there other ways of stopping the boats, stopping drownings at sea, which have integrity and which are consistent with international law?' But we haven't done that."

label.en: How many immigrants should Australia admit?

analystStatement.en: Net migration to Australia reached almost 1 million people in Labor’s first two years – 70 per cent higher than in any previous two-year period. A new person is migrating to Australia every 46 seconds. This is unsustainable and is severely impacting our social and economic infrastructure. [...] A Dutton Coalition Government will: Urgently address the record levels of migration intake under Labor by reducing the permanent migration intake by 25 per cent.

partyStatement.en: "We will reduce the permanent migration program by 25 per cent – from 185,000 to 140,000 for the first two years in recognition of the urgency of this crisis. The program will then increase to 150,000 in year three and 160,000 in year four."

analystStatement.en: [Prime Minister Anthony Albanese]: "You know, we are fixing the mess on migration that we inherited. The numbers are expected to be cut by half over the coming year [2024] [...] We're doing that in order to ensure that migration is at appropriate levels, but so that we continue to get as well, we need to have the skilled workers coming in, in construction, in nursing, in some of these areas that are needed."

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government is taking action to fix the broken migration system we inherited from the former Liberal Government and bring migration back down to sustainable, normal levels after the spike post-pandemic. As a result of  Government action, net migration has passed its peak.

analystStatement.en: The Australian Greens want: A permanent migration program for refugees and migrants to Australia that prioritises family reunion and humanitarian programs; Refugee and migrant programs that are equitable, non-discriminatory, affordable, and facilitate resettlement to Australia within a reasonable time frame.

partyStatement.en: Under the policies of the Liberals and Labor, our immigration system has become cruel and dysfunctional, prioritising borders and economics over people and communities. The Greens are committed to rebuilding an immigration system that reflects these core Australian values—welcoming refugees with dignity, supporting families with fairness, and fostering social inclusion. We are working to deliver a system that strengthens our communities, upholds human rights, and collaborates with our region to create lasting, cooperative solutions for those seeking safety and a new life.

analystStatement.en: Zero-net immigration throughout COVID illustrated how putting the brakes on migration reduced congestion on our roads and allowed Government services to focus on Australians. One Nation will extend its zero-net migration policy and focus on permitting only highly skilled migrants from culturally cohesive countries into Australia.

Russell Broadbent: "Labor's immigration policy—bringing in 518,000 people in 2022-23—has served only to inflame [the housing crisis] to the point where now homeownership is unaffordable for the vast majority of the Australian population."

Kate Chaney: "A temporary ban on the foreign purchase of residential property is one lever. It won't solve the whole piece [of the housing crisis], but it is part of the toolkit. I was initially concerned about this because it can come across as being xenophobic. I'm not against immigration . This is a short-term response to a crisis that we have at the moment."

partyStatement.en: Immigrants have always been part of Australia's prosperity and strength. As the Covid spike ends and we return to long term trends, we should use a long term forecast for economic and social planning.
The focus should be on skilled migration and particular skills gaps.

analystStatement.en: Helen Haines: "Families desperate to begin their lives together should be reunited as quickly as possible. Migration has long been the key to Australia's economic success. The PM has predicted an 85 per cent drop in net migration this financial year. Migration will be crucial in the COVID recovery, and, when the borders open up, we should prioritise partner visas. We should welcome people who have chosen Australia as their new home, with a partner already in the community. They have a long-term plan and will invest in housing and their children's education. We should encourage them to move to regional Australia. The country, as I can attest, is a great place to grow up. Let's get them here."

Dai Le [Independent]: "My electorate of Fowler has been a settlement city. More than 70 per cent of our population have parents born overseas or people speaking a language other than English. We are a settlement electorate, and we're proud of that. As a former refugee myself, I know that people like me have contributed so much to the rich cultural tapestry of Fowler, but our area is buckling from the pressure of having to accommodate more people with very little infrastructure support from successive governments."

Dr [Monique] Ryan: "Presenting the Education Services for Overseas Students Amendment (Quality and Integrity) Bill 2024 as an education bill is a misrepresentation. This bill reflects the fact that the sector has become an unwilling and unfortunate victim of the major parties' race to the bottom on immigration numbers. It is indeed a very sad day when we see our major political parties competing to damage an important Australian growth sector and export industry."
Dr [Sophie] Scamps: "What are the solutions [to the housing crisis]? Yes, we do need to address immigration levels, and this is happening."

Ms [Allegra] Spender: "Migration is central to the story of Australia. As the daughter of a migrant , I know firsthand the contribution that migrants make to our wonderful and diverse society and the opportunities Australia can provide for those who come to our shores to work, study and live."

Immigration needs to be managed in an orderly and measured way to ensure population levels can be sustainably supported, in step with infrastructure, transport, housing and investment. With population growth, more pressure is put on our natural environment due to urbanisation, pollution and biodiversity loss. Population increases must be aligned with monitoring and long-term sustainability of our natural environment.

partyStatement.en: Immigration is a necessary way to lift Australia's productivity, help to contribute to the innovation of our small businesses and alleviate worker shortages in key industries, such as aged care. However, it needs to be managed in an orderly and measured way to ensure population levels can be sustainably supported, in step with infrastructure, transport, housing and investment.

Australia needs a strong and well-planed migration program, but only insofar as the country can effectively sustain, especially with regards to the environment, housing, healthcare and infrastructure.

analystStatement.en: KAP Federal Member for Kennedy Bob Katter [...] said [...] "Everyone in this country knows the problem is not simply just the “ghost universities”. It goes much further than that. The government clearly, in trying to make it look like they're doing something about immigration, is dealing with two per cent of the problem instead of the 98 per cent of the problem they should be dealing with. This country doesn't want any immigrants at present —54,000 families can't find a home in this country, yet the government continues to bring in half a million people.”

partyStatement.en: Migration must be immediately stopped and money saved reallocated to the support of Australian families. Migration can be restarted once housing and the cost of living has stablised.

Our immigration intake should be matched to our capacity to accommodate new migrants, and balanced with social and economic benefits. We must remember Australia is a nation with finite and fragile environmental resources and increasing population puts pressure on those resources.

label.en: Asylum seekers who arrive by boat should be held in offshore detention centres while their claims are being processed.

analystStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition will [...] Build on the success of Operation Sovereign Borders to expand and enhance our border security to stop people smuggling and secure our borders.

partyStatement.en: A Dutton Coalition Government will build on the success of Operation Sovereign Borders to expand and enhance our border security to stop people smuggling and secure our borders. The Coalition is strongly committed to turnbacks where it is safe to do so - these formed an important part of the former Coalition Government’s successful border protection policy Operation Sovereign Borders (OSB).  The three pillars of OSB – Temporary Protection Visas, Regional Processing and turnbacks where it is safe to do so –  successfully halted the people smugglers, stopped the deaths at sea and removed all the children from detention.

analystStatement.en: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the arrival of a boat carrying several asylum seekers to Western Australia's far north coast is "unfortunate" but not a failure of Operation Sovereign Borders. The federal opposition has gone on the offensive over the arrival of 39 men who say they travelled by boat from Indonesia to remote communities in WA's north-west on Friday. It accuses the government of short-changing the department and allowing surveillance operations to fail. [...] Mr Albanese rubbished those suggestions, saying the government had not cut funding to the Australian Border Force (ABF) and had maintained offshore processing programs. "It is working. That's why they're in Nauru. That's the whole point, the whole point," Mr Albanese told the Australian Radio Network. [...] "What's important is that the system is in place so that people who arrive as unauthorised arrivals by boat won't be allowed to settle here. That's my government's policy."

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government believes as a nation we must not harm people seeking refuge. Offshore regional processing is a key pillar of our border security. Regional processing countries are responsible for determining how they manage people while their claims are being assessed, including whether they should be in detention.

analystStatement.en: [The] Greens have a plan to: End offshore detention on Manus Island and Nauru, bringing refugees to safety and freedom in Australia, and ensuring we create a fairer and safer system that helps more people and meets our international obligations.

partyStatement.en: Under the policies of the Liberals and Labor, our immigration system has become cruel and dysfunctional, prioritising borders and economics over people and communities. The Greens are committed to rebuilding an immigration system that reflects these core Australian values—welcoming refugees with dignity, supporting families with fairness, and fostering social inclusion. We are working to deliver a system that strengthens our communities, upholds human rights, and collaborates with our region to create lasting, cooperative solutions for those seeking safety and a new life.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "Only by committing to offshore processing in places like Nauru can we arrest the tide of smuggled people that would override our borders."

Russell Broadbent: "I am therefore pleased to present this petition: [...] We therefore ask the House to: increase the number of refugees to be accepted for resettlement; abolish closed detention centres and resettle those living there in Australia. As an alternative, establish reception centres on the mainland to allow us to provide support to the most vulnerable process people in a timely and humane way no matter how they arrive and ensure that there is a fair and adequate appeal system; treat every refugee and every asylum seeker as you would want a citizen of Australia to be treated if they were in the same situation."

Kate Chaney: "There remains a significant sum allocated for maintaining detention centres in Nauru as a deterrent. I would prefer to see this go and for Australia to comply with its international legal obligations in relation to asylum seekers."

partyStatement.en: This shifts the problem to other countries, rather than addressing it directly and is very expensive.

analystStatement.en: If elected, I would seek to implement the following: End indefinite hotel detention immediately [...] Further, I will seek an independent review of the current system to consider its cost to taxpayers and humanitarian impact. Terms of reference to include the following: Ending offshore detention based on cost benefit analysis

partyStatement.en: Offshore detention doesnt stack up  from either a cost or human rights point of view. If it is to continue the process must be strictly limited to a short time frame.

analystStatement.en: Helen Haines: "When it comes to our immigration policies I and many other Australians are left asking the simple question of who we are as a country. I bring the voices of so many people in my electorate who call for an end to the human suffering that is caused through indefinite detention of asylum seekers and refugees both onshore and offshore."

Dai Le [Independent]: "I support some form of processing, but in a fair way, because we do need to ensure genuine refugees can get the opportunity to be resettled. Continuing to use Nauru for offshore detention in its current state, keeping 65 people who, I believe, have been in detention for a long time—nearly 10 years—just does not make sense."

[Monique Ryan]: "We have an opportunity to put an end to offshore processing and indefinite detention and to give a new beginning to the 30,000 people stuck on precarious temporary visas, welcoming them with permanent protection."
Dr [Sophie] Scamps: "I rise on the matter of public importance: the need for the government to urgently end the practice of indefinite detention of refugees both offshore and onshore."

I'm focussed on [...] Compassionate treatment of refugees – including ending the uncertainty for eight thousand asylum seekers living in limbo for a decade, introducing a 90-day limit on detention, and banning detention of children.

partyStatement.en: Asylum seekers must be processed quickly and held humanely. Australia has fallen short of these standards in the past.

analystStatement.en: We must fight for equity and human rights for all, ensuring everyone is empowered to be active, visible and respected. This includes ending the wasteful spending on the offshore detention of refugees and seeking alternative solutions to detention through resettlement in community or through diplomatic solutions with other countries such as New Zealand, the US and Canada.

partyStatement.en: We must end offshore detention, from both a humanitarian perspective and an economic perspective. In the FY24/25 Budget, offshore detention cost Australia $604.4 million - an astronomical amount for just 979 people.

analystStatement.en: [Andrew Wilkie]: "The government would say, the minister would say, that the current regime of Operation Sovereign Borders and offshore processing works and has stopped the boats. But the end does not justify the means, in particular when there are other approaches we should be considering and exploring. Four months ago there was an opportunity for us to come into this place and debate and explore the possibility of other responses to irregular immigrants, to ask ourselves, 'Are there other ways of stopping the boats, stopping drownings at sea, which have integrity and which are consistent with international law?' But we haven't done that."

label.en: Australia Day should continue to be celebrated on January 26.

analystStatement.en: [Opposition Leader Peter] Dutton was asked whether he would legislate to permanently recognise January 26 as Australia Day. “I’m happy to look at the suggestion and happy to make sure that we continue to be proud of who we are as a country,” he said. [...] “If people don't want to celebrate Australia Day, that's entirely their choice. I'm comfortable with that and relaxed with it. That's their decision,” Mr Dutton said. “But I don't want to be told by woke CEOs and a weak Prime Minister that I can't celebrate Australia Day.”

partyStatement.en: The Coalition believes on 26 January we should unashamedly celebrate the achievements of modern Australia. Australians should recognise the good and bad in our history and there is no denying 26 January 1788 was a moment of immense significance that should not be ignored, by changing the date of a public holiday. It also has a poignancy for the many migrants who become Australian citizens every year on this date.

analystStatement.en: Australia Day should remain on 26 January, according to Labor leader Anthony Albanese. Despite acknowledging the “devastating impact” the arrival of the First Fleet had on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and culture, when asked in an interview with Macquarie Radio on Thursday whether he was supportive of keeping Australia Day on the current date, Mr Albanese said: "Yes, I am".

partyStatement.en: The Prime Minister has said Australia Day is an opportunity to celebrate everything we've built together and be optimistic for the future we can shape together.

analystStatement.en: For many, January 26 is not a day of celebration. It is a day of mourning - one that marks the survival and the resistance First Nations people have always shown. Australia has a strong bla[c]k history. First Peoples connection to culture, country and Language has endured throughout ongoing colonisation. It is important on days like this to tell the truth about our past, and the community to listen, so that we can move forward together. Collectively, we can build a shared vision for this country, respecting and reconciling our past means acknowledging that our sovereignty has never been ceded.

partyStatement.en: 26 January is not a day of celebration. It is a day commemorating two hundred years of dispossession, inequality and destruction that continues to this day. We mourn the attempted destruction of First Nations languages and culture, the theft of Country and songlines, and the loss of children who were stolen from their families. We mourn for those who have died and those who still suffer injustices and inequality in systems built to keep First Nations people disenfranchised here in Australia and around the world.

analystStatement.en: Australia Day always was and always should be on January 26. It holds a special place in the hearts of Australians. It’s a day to celebrate our nation’s rich history, Aussie culture, and shared achievements. One Nation firmly supports keeping Australia Day on this important date, recognising it as a unifying moment for all Australians to reflect on our country’s journey and look forward to a brighter future.

Russell Broadbent: "This Australia Day there's been quite a lot of criticism around celebrating Australia today. Well, I just want to say to you that we've got these stickers now and it says "Proud Australian; Proud of our Nation"."

partyStatement.en: Australia Day should be held on a unifying date that can be celebrated by all.

analystStatement.en: Dai Le [Independent]: "In our community in Fowler in Western Sydney we've always celebrated Australia Day [...] So we celebrate that and we acknowledge that, but we also acknowledge our history [...] There are going to be issues, but we need to have a conversation whereby we acknowledge Australia Day as Australia Day."
[Monique Ryan]: 26 January is a complex day for many Australians. I’m proud to be Australian, but I know that for many of us, particularly those from First Nations communities, today is a sad day.

partyStatement.en: I don't think this is an issue we need to decide quickly. In my personal view, January 26 is a significant date that should be commemorated but is too divisive to be celebrated as our national day.

For First Nations Australians, January 26 is a day of mourning of the history of colonisation within our country. Instead, Australia's day of national significance should fall on a date where all Australians can celebrate. However, there is little national consensus about which date our national day should be observed.

analystStatement.en: From national supermarkets refusing to stock Australia Day merchandise to government departments banning any display of the flag, Mr Katter said that the nation has been led down a dark path by minority interest groups. "The Department of Home Affairs issued instructions that there will be no Australian flags in any of their buildings," Mr Katter said, referring to actions taken by the federal government department late last year. "Enough is enough, can you believe an Australian government department stifling patriotism? We are Australian. We are allowed to be proud," Katter declared. Mr Katter, who "celebrates Australia Day every day", plans to bring the Allegiance to Australia Bill 2025 to Parliament at the earliest possible opportunity.
Happy #australiaday ! For me, today is a day of thanks and grace that I am a citizen of the best nation on earth.

label.en: Australia should set up a Truth and Justice Commission to look into how the government has mistreated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

analystStatement.en: The opposition leader, Peter Dutton, said that if he won office, there would be no makarrata, or truth-telling.

partyStatement.en: The Australian people rejected the Uluru Statement, calling for "Voice, Treaty, Truth" pursued by Anthony Albanese. Unlike Labor, the Coalition will focus on practical action for Indigenous Australians, rather than symbolism and tokenism. We will focus our efforts on addressing the significant disadvantage and neglect within regional and remote Indigenous communities. Labor's sole focus was the Voice to Parliament, rather than practical action to address the varied instances of inequality, poverty and neglect in Indigenous Australia.

analystStatement.en: Since the failed referendum, the government’s line has been that it is taking time to consult on the way forward in Indigenous policy. In the Uluru statement from the heart, which on election night Anthony Albanese committed to implementing “in full”, a Makarrata commission was proposed to oversee a process of treaty making and truth telling. [...] But that was contingent on a successful public vote to set up the voice to parliament. Last month, Albanese said he’d go to the Garma festival in Arnhem Land again this August to talk to Yolngu leaders. “I’ll … sit down with people and talk about a way forward. One of the things that we wanted to do, the whole point of the voice, was listening to people in communities, rather than people in Canberra making decisions going forward, and that’s what we’ve been doing,” Albanese said in June. The [Former] Indigenous Australians minister, Linda Burney, said the government was committed to the principles of truth-telling and Makarrata, but that there were a “variety of views on how to move forward”.

partyStatement.en: Minister McCarthy warns weaponisation that occurred through the referendum  could occur with truth-telling without bipartisanship. State and territory processes underway.

analystStatement.en: The Greens have introduced a bill to set up a federal truth and justice commission, nine months on from the defeat of the voice to parliament referendum. [...] Their bill seeks to establish a truth and justice commission with 10 members – one from each state and territory, and two chief commissioners – appointed jointly by the attorney general and the minister for Indigenous affairs. The “majority” of the members would be First Nations peoples. Commissioners would serve a two-year term and could be reappointed for a second term only. The commission would investigate historical and ongoing “systemic injustices perpetrated by the commonwealth government” and its agencies, and report on how those injustices would be “acknowledged and redressed in a culturally appropriate way”. It would be required to report its findings and recommendations within four years. It would also have coercive power to compel a witness to attend a hearing, to give evidence and to produce documents, and could issue search warrants.

partyStatement.en: Everyone who calls Australia home needs to understand how this country was established and the impacts that this has had and continues to have on the First Peoples of this country. Any Treaty or Treaties must be based on the truth of our past. The referendum campaign clearly showed that there is a compelling case for truth-telling and treaty-making to deliver hope, justice and pathways towards healing for the nation. The Greens' plan: Establish a National Truth and Justice Commission to acknowledge and document historic and ongoing injustices experienced by First Nations peoples; Allocate $250 million in funding to the Commission to hold hearings, compile reports, and develop processes for embedding localised truth-telling across the country; Engage communities in grassroots consultation on models for a national treaty or treaties, ensuring collaboration with First Nations peoples, governments, and key stakeholders throughout the process.

analystStatement.en: [One Nation Leader] Pauline Hanson: "The Prime Minister's Voice to Parliament was overwhelmingly thrown out by Australians, as it should have been. It was divisive, insulting and full of lies that were only said to further pit one Australian against another with more rights and privileges. The PM claims now that he didn't advocate for a Makarrata Commission—another lie. He endorsed and promised the Uluru Statement from the Heart in full, which included the Makarrata and truth-telling."

partyStatement.en: In the current political context, proceeding with this could be counterproductive as it could reignite culture wars, but the appropriateness of such a commission should be reviewed in future years.

analystStatement.en: I support the Uluru Statement from the Heart and substantive, constitutional recognition of Australia’s First Nations people. I support Truth Telling processes, and in line with the Statement, structural reform so that, ‘this ancient sovereignty can shine through as a fuller expression of Australia’s nationhood.’ A First Nations Voice in the Constitution would create a direct line of communication between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and the parliament, creating specific input into policy. This is an important step towards self determination for First Nations Australians.

partyStatement.en: Given this is happening at state level I have a question about whether it needs to be duplicated federally.
Australians need to understand our history and the impact past events still have today.
I support the full implementation of the Uluru Statement, which includes the Makarrata Commission to oversee the process of truth-telling about our history.
The remote First Australian communities need their basic nutritional requirements met through market gardens, not Canberra-based bureaucratic naval-gazing.
I support practical measures that close the gap in the life expectancy and life outcomes between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians.

label.en: Australia should always fly the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags alongside the Australian flag in official settings.

analystStatement.en: “Now, we should have respect for the Indigenous flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag, but they are not our national flags. I think the prime minister sends a very confusing message.” [...] “I just don’t think that we can be a united nation and a unified nation without the thought of standing behind anything other than one flag,” [Peter Dutton] said.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition deeply respects the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags. There will be occasions where it is appropriate for the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags to fly alongside the Australian flag. However, every other civilisation, every other western country unites under one flag and we have one national flag, the Australian flag, which will always be flown in official settings and in front of which a Prime Minister Dutton would stand to demonstrate that we are one united people, all of equal value.

analystStatement.en: When Anthony Albanese took to the podium for his first press conference as Prime Minister at Parliament House, he stood not in front of one flag, but three. The Australian national flag. The Australian Aboriginal flag. The Torres Strait Islander flag. To some, this change may have appeared insignificant. To others it instantly represented another step towards greater inclusion. A reminder of where we are as a nation, and where we can walk to together.

partyStatement.en: The Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Flag were proclaimed flags of Australia under section 5 of the Flags Act 1953 on 14 July 1995. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander culture is the oldest continuing culture in the world and Australians should take great pride in that.

analystStatement.en: The Greens Let’s Fly the Flags for Truth and Justice campaign shows solidarity with First Nations peoples and that we will never accept Trump-style politics and engage in the culture wars. Both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags are recognised as national flags and are used to ensure we recognise, and respect, the sovereignty of First Peoples of Australia.

partyStatement.en: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags are recognised as national flags and are used to ensure we recognise the sovereignty of the First Peoples of Australia. We are a culturally diverse and vibrant nation of many people from so many backgrounds, but as Australians we are connected to the oldest living cultures in the world. These flags symbolise our commitment to unity and reconciling our nation's history.

analystStatement.en: One Nation leader Pauline Hanson [...] highlights the importance of national unity, criticising the display of multiple flags in Parliament and public spaces, emphasising that one flag represents all Australians.

partyStatement.en: This is not 'always' appropriate as we have one national flag, but there are many occasions when displaying both is appropriate, as as sign of respect and recognition.
Flying all of the Australian flags, including the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags, is an important unifying gesture.

The Australian flag should fly alongside the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags in domestic settings, but it may be inappropriate in other settings, such as international delegations and international sporting events, where the Australian flag should be standalone.

analystStatement.en: Mr Katter, who "celebrates Australia Day every day", plans to bring the Allegiance to Australia Bill 2025 to Parliament at the earliest possible opportunity. [...] The pledge of allegiance to Australia would mean the recital of the verse: "I pledge allegiance to the Flag of Australia, and to the nation for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all."

partyStatement.en: Why is the Eureka flag not listed in this debate?
This should be at the discretion of the flag bearer.

label.en: Employees should have the right to refuse work calls and emails outside of their working hours.

analystStatement.en: Opposition Leader Peter Dutton has sworn to repeal laws that will give workers the right to ignore unreasonable out-of-hours communications from their bosses if the Coalition wins the next federal election. [...] Mr Dutton says even corrected, the laws will be damaging to relations between employers and employees, and make the task of restarting productivity growth even more difficult. Asked on Sky News if his party would repeal the "right to disconnect" if it won government, Mr Dutton responded with an emphatic: "Yes we will."

partyStatement.en: Employees should not have to work unreasonable overtime, and this protection is already provided for in the Fair Work Act. Small businesses need to have the freedom to manage their workforce efficiently and workers need to have the flexibility to juggle their professional and personal lives without the constraints of excessive regulation.  Labor’s misguided “right to disconnect” laws are confusing to both employers and employees, with small businesses unsure about whether they will face significant fines for contacting their employees on weekends, even if it is to offer an extra shift or ask a simple question about a workplace matter.

analystStatement.en: Workers will soon have the right to ignore unreasonable calls and emails outside their rostered shifts, after the government’s legislation cleared parliament on Thursday. [...] Anthony Albanese said on Sunday that Dutton’s opposition to the right-to-disconnect laws, and initial hesitance in backing reforms to stage three tax cuts, showed he “wants people to work longer, for less”. “What Peter Dutton wants is lower wages, more taxes on low and middle income Australians, and to continue to wind back any reforms that are made in the interests of working people,” the prime minister said.

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government has legislated a Right to Disconnect, which acts as a protection against disciplinary action if an employee refuses to answer calls or emails after hours.

analystStatement.en: Following months of negotiations with the government and the crossbench, the Greens have secured support in their push for a legislated right to disconnect for workers. As a long-time campaign and demand of the Greens, this win allows workers to ignore contact from their employers outside of work hours, unless they are paid for it.

partyStatement.en: In February 2024, following months of negotiations with the government and the crossbench, the Greens secured support in their push for a legislated right to disconnect for workers. As a long-time campaign and demand of the Greens, this win allows workers to ignore contact from their employers outside of work hours, unless they are paid for it. The amendments to the Fair Work Legislation Amendment (Closing Loopholes No. 2) Bill 2023 will give employees an enforceable right to refuse contact from their employer out of hours unless that refusal is unreasonable. Where the issue cannot be resolved at the workplace, and the behaviour continues, the Fair Work Commission can issue stop orders. If they are breached, the normal civil remedies of the Fair Work system will apply. Factors like the reason for contact, the level of contact, compensation, job role and responsibility, and workers’ personal circumstances will be taken into account in deciding what is reasonable contact.

analystStatement.en: The Labor Party’s arrogance towards democracy knows no bounds, and now their arrogance will have extreme consequences. It turns out they ‘accidentally’ voted for legislation yesterday that would put a business owner in jail if that employer calls one of their employees out of hours. It’s a story that would be funny if were not so serious!

partyStatement.en: Employers and employees should be able to work out appropriate expectations between themselves, depending on the nature of their work.
Depends on the industry, the role, the remuneration and a range of other factors.

analystStatement.en: Coming into effect from Aug 26, 2025, this legislation could create conflict in workplaces where flexibility already works.

partyStatement.en: Workers and employers of course need to find a balance around after-hours expectations. That will be different for each job, so this is best done case-by-case rather than by blanket legislation.

The increased availability of technology has afforded employees more freedom to work unusual hours or to not be physically onsite but also assured employers that they are contactable if needed. This shows there is a level of nuance that is worthy of greater scrutiny in order to get policy setting right, which includes the balance of flexibility with being connected.
This should not require regulation. Flexibility in the workplace should be allowed and appropriately compensated for.
This is dependent on the individual job role and agreements employees make with their respective employer.

label.en: Cannabis should be legalised for recreational use.

analystStatement.en: Australia’s third-largest political party, the Greens, lodged a bill to legalise the drug this year. […] With Labor indicating it does not support the bill at this stage, this leaves the support of the Coalition, which was actually the party that paved the way for legalised medical marijuana back in 2016. Coalition member and shadow attorney-general Michaelia Cash told ABC News she “fundamentally disagrees” with going further. “I have spoken to many parents over many years in relation to their children who have utilised drugs and even cannabis. And those who’ve had detrimental effects,” she says.

partyStatement.en: The Coalition does not support measures that increase the availability and consumption of illicit drugs, or measures which imply that the use of illicit drugs is safe.

analystStatement.en: [Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate Senator Don Farrell]: "The government does not support this bill, the Legalising Cannabis Bill 2023. Laws dealing with the recreational possession and use of cannabis are matters for the states and territories."

partyStatement.en: Laws dealing with the recreational possession and use of cannabis are essentially a matter for the states and territories.

analystStatement.en: Today the Greens Legalising Cannabis Bill 2023 came to a vote in the Senate and was disappointingly blocked by the Labor and Coalition parties in a 13 to 24 vote against progress. Nevertheless this is a historic day. It’s the first time the Federal Parliament has voted on a plan to legalise cannabis across the country … and it won’t be the last. Greens Senator and Justice Spokesperson David Shoebridge said: “We took a big step today from treating cannabis as part of the failing ‘war on drugs’ and instead putting forward a model that is safer, reduces harms and delivers for the millions of Australians who just want us to legalize it!"

partyStatement.en: The Australian Greens are moving ahead with the first national plan to legalise cannabis. Senator David Shoebridge, on behalf of the Greens, has obtained constitutional law advice that shows how the Federal Parliament can legalise cannabis for adult use across the country. The world is rapidly moving away from the damaging criminal and policing approach to cannabis. Australia risks being left behind if we wait for piecemeal reform through the states and territories that may well leave millions of Australians behind. Using the national reach of the Federal Parliament we can legalise it, everywhere all at once, and bring in billions of dollars of much needed new public revenue at the same time.

analystStatement.en: One Nation Chief of Staff James Ashby says legalising cannabis for recreational use is a “bad recipe” for Australia. Mr Ashby joined Sky News host Peta Credlin to discuss the latest with the ongoing debate over whether cannabis should be legalised for recreational use across Australia. “I’ve always advocated for the use of medicinal cannabis when it comes to people who’ve got chronic illness, where they’re failing in life in the sense that they’re going to die of cancer or something like that,” he said. “It’s been proven to work very well. But opening this full slather and allowing people to just have a smoke whenever they choose – I’ve seen the consequences of this with schoolmates that I went to school with.”

partyStatement.en: I note this is fundamentally a state issue.
As a doctor I witnessed the harms of overuse of cannabis.
Let a thousand blossoms bloom as far I'm concerned...but I ain't spendin' any time on it.

label.en: How much tax should large corporations pay?

analystStatement.en: Taxation is the killer of aspiration and the best reward for hard work is lower taxes. [...] The private sector should drive economic growth, with the role of government to support Australian industry and the economy by being efficient and not creating obstacles to success.

partyStatement.en: Large corporations and multinationals should pay their fair share of tax. The previous Coalition government implemented over a dozen measures, including our Multinational Anti-Avoidance Law that brought over $7 billion a year back into the tax net. We will prioritise tax relief for Australia's millions of small and medium businesses that employ almost half of all employees. This includes expanding the instant asset write off to $30,000 and making it ongoing; and, for two years, allowing small firms to deduct up to $20,000 of business-related meal expenses, to help them weather Labor's record insolvency crisis. The Coalition has no plans to reduce the company tax rate for large corporations.

analystStatement.en: Treasurer Jim Chalmers vowed not to follow US president-elect Donald Trump’s lead to cut the corporate tax rate. [...] Dr Chalmers said the government would resist pressure from business and taxation experts to cut Australia’s 30 per cent corporate tax rate, despite Mr Trump’s plans for a 15 per cent level. [...] Dr Chalmers said Labor wasn’t planning any change, and cautioned that investors had other priorities for reform. ”We’re not planning to cut the company tax rate, the headline company tax rate, but there’s a heap of reform that we’re doing when it comes to the taxes in our business,” he added. “You know, the production tax credits, parts of our Future Made in Australia policy, the instant asset write-off for smaller businesses. There has been an element of reform, but I understand and accept that we haven’t been proposing anything like what President Trump has been proposing.”

partyStatement.en: The Albanese Government is improving the fairness in the tax system by making multinationals pay their fair share - there is no place for tax evasion. Multinational companies making a profit in Australia should pay tax on those profits in Australia. We have strengthened global corporate tax transparency and implemented a new global minimum tax and domestic minimum tax for multinationals.

analystStatement.en: The Greens have a fully-costed plan to tackle the cost of living crisis at its roots by making big corporations and billionaires pay their fair share. [...] We’ll raise over $514 billion in revenue to fund this by: Introducing a 40% tax on excess profits for big corporations with over $100 million in turnover[;] Stopping big oil & gas corporations paying $0 in tax by closing loopholes – and raising royalties so Australia gets its fair share from resources owned by the public[;] Tackling multinational tax avoidance.

partyStatement.en: The Greens will take a series of ‘Robin Hood reforms’ to the next election, including a 40% tax on the excessive profits of big corporations to fund significant cost of living support. Independently costed by the PBO, the Greens’ Big Corporations Tax package will raise $514b over the next decade. It ensures that big corporations who make excessive profits pay a higher share of tax on these excessive profits.

analystStatement.en: We will maintain our opposition to the reintroduction of death duties and pursue a tax regime that ensures multi-national businesses pay their fair share of tax while operating within Australia.

partyStatement.en: Our corporate tax framework needs to be internationally competitive to attract foreign investment.

analystStatement.en: Zoe Daniel: "We must get serious about ensuring that big corporations making huge profits pay their fair share. Other countries do it, yet we're so frightened of upsetting the multinationals that we don't. I've been advocating for a properly funded properly resourced inquiry into Tax and Revenue reform with everything on the table since before the last election"

partyStatement.en: Especially fossil fuel exporters on windfall profits, and social media companies which offshore their profits from the Australian market.
Depends on the type of corporation and the nature of the tax.

The business sector should pay about the same amount of tax as currently, but the system should move to better incentivise innovation and investment, and extract a fairer return from our natural resources.

The Australian Taxation Office's annual tax transparency report revealed the amount of tax paid by some 2,468 large-to-medium corporation entities, and it showed that no tax was paid by nearly one-third. More than half of the mining, energy and water companies included in the report paid by no income tax in 2020-21.
